subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY

speechtext: The House resumed, from Wednesday, July 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Drury that Bill C-196, respecting the 1976 summer Olympic games, be read the third time and do pass; and the amendment thereto of Mr. Peters (page 5975).

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was saying yesterday that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been either naive or deceptive with this House and the people of Canada during the past five years with respect to the financing of the 1976 summer Olympics. In many ways he could be likened to a plant manager who under questioning about a pet project that the manager seems interested in, tells his employers, who may have heard rumours to the contrary for five years, that he has made no special business concessions, has agreed to no special contributions, commitments or assistance and has not agreed to give direct financial assistance. Finally he states categorically that the project will not cost the employers a penny.
Then the manager explains at the last moment that he has agreed to turn over the bulk of his plant's production-which in this case is the Royal Canadian Mint-for four years. The plant is to be run at four times its normal volume on a non-profit basis, all of the net proceeds from the special run will be going to his pet project. To make matters worse, the employers find out that while they will make nothing out of the run, they will be contingently liable with respect to all sales made during the four-year period. I suggest the employers in such a position would first fire the employee and then make the best of the bad deal to which they had been committed by the fired employee. In this case we will have to wait for the voters who, hopefully, will do the firing of the Prime Minister. In the meantime it is up to this House, and particularly the opposition, to make the best of a bad deal.


Olympic Bill
I feel that members of the NDP have not acted responsibly in this matter. As was pointed out yesterday, representatives of that party on February 2 said they were in favour of the Olympics and in favour of the coinage and stamp issue that was contemplated and finally announced by the Prime Minister for the first time on that date. The NDP want the luxury of disassociating themselves from this Olympics deal, now that they know the nation is hooked. Whether we like it or not, the nation has been hooked by a Prime Minister whom the NDP has propped up for nine months. The nation has been hooked by a Prime Minister who, because of the NDP vote in committee on July 11, was not invited to appear before the committee and required to explain how he got the country into the position of having to turn the net proceeds from our Mint over to a private corporation for four years. He should have been required to explain why he spent four years denying what was going on, and why he now persists in pretending that what is happening is not happening.
The Conservative's proposal to have the Prime Minister appear before the committee was turned down as a result of a vote taken in committee. Eight of our members voted unanimously for the Prime Minister to appear before the committee, but the Liberal and NDP representatives on the committee said that in no way would that happen and voted against hearing the Prime Minister. It was a recorded vote.
Consider the inconsistency of the NDP. They made a statement on February 2. Yesterday one NDP member admitted that they had changed direction in the subsequent speech made on June 28. That hon. member ought to read the report of the committee meeting that occurred subsequent to June 28. He would see the direction that his party took that evening. As I said, the NDP voted against hearing the Prime Minister in committee. When my party moved an amendment, hoping to tidy up this bill and limit to $250 million the amount the Olympic corporation may get from the coinage issued plus another $10 million from the stamp issue, one or two Liberal members voted for the proposal. But not the Prime Minister's most trusted allies, the NDP. They did not vote for it.
At that time one of the NDP members of the committee made the startling comment, recorded at page 40:48 of the committee proceedings, that the limit of $250 million was unnecessarily rigid. Another of their spokesmen on the committee said he could not see voting to limit this amount because in the unlikely event that they should make a profit of the kind that had been suggested, then more power to them. He was speaking of the Olympic corporation. Earlier that member had said, as recorded at page 40:50 of the committee proceedings, that those who take the risks should also have the opportunity of receiving whatever profit there may be.
For reasons that will become evident later in my address, it was unfortunate that the committee was not allowed to question the Prime Minister. So that hon. members may know the thinking of the sponsor of this bill, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), they should know that during the committee hearings he said that the Prime Minister did not have much to add to this particular bill nor any information regarding it. When asked if the
|Mr. Stevens.]
Prime Minister would appear before the committee, the President of the Treasury Board said the Prime Minister's time "is more valuable." This is recorded at page 38:17 of the committee proceedings.
The comment made by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) as recorded at page 38:23 of the committee proceedings is interesting by way of background information. When we were discussing whether the Prime Minister should appear at committee, the hon. member said, as translated:
-we also know, and many of us will not admit it, perfectly well there were frequent meetings between the Prime Minister of Canada and Mr. Drapeau; and we know perfectly well if the political context, since October 30, were different, if we had a majority government, Canada's commitment would have been on a much broader scale than it is now. We must admit it, and of course a compromise has to be found.
Perhaps unwittingly, or possibly with much more knowledge than many of us have in this chamber, I believe the hon. member put his finger on the question. If I may, I would like to trace through what is reported in Hansard, including documents that have been tabled, to show the contradictory position that has been taken by the government, particularly by the Prime Minister, with regard to this matter.
Before commencing to do so, I think it is wise to get our terms of reference accurate because in the quotations I intend to refer to we will find words such as "coinage", "financial", "special" and "contribution" used in very loose terms. It is wise to put on the record how the Oxford dictionary defines these words. "Financial" is defined as pertaining to revenue or money matters. "Money" is defined as current coin, coin and promissory documents representing it. "Coin" is defined as a piece of metal made into money by official stamp, metal money, money. "Contribute" is defined as to pay, furnish, that is, to contribute to a common fund. "Contribution" is defined as the act of contributing. Finally, "special" is defined as being of a particular kind, peculiar, not general.
In the records that have either been tabled in the House or printed in Hansard, the first reference to the 1976 summer Olympics is a letter to the then minister of national health and welfare from the mayor of Montreal, dated November 18, 1968. In that letter the mayor stated he had just read Mr. Munro's letter of October 25. He stated it seemed to sum up in substance the discussions they held in Mexico City on Friday, October 11, 1968. I am sorry we do not know what those discussions were. The mayor of Montreal then attempted to summarize what he considered to be the Olympic financing plans. In the body of the letter he stated:
We believe that the necessary expenses will be financed by public authorities, under existing legislation-
This I emphasize:
-or under legislation which could be passed anyway for all kinds of related purposes-
Was the mayor of Montreal a little psychic as far back as 1968 in referring to new legislation which was introduced in 1973 for all kinds of related purposes, namely, coins, stamps and lotteries? In another paragraph of the same letter he said:


-we do not feel we will have to ask governments at higher levels for special grants in order to hold the 1976 Olympics- We are not giving up, however, the right to any advantages which might be extended to us under existing or future legislation.
The words "future legislation" are repeated several times throughout the correspondence. I find it interesting that in all the government's correspondence to the Montreal organizers of the Olympics not once is the simple question asked: What future legislation do you mean? Is it that the federal authorities knew what the mayor meant? In any event, the Olympic organizers always qualified their statements by saying they wished to keep their option open concerning future legislation.
We then come to two more letters. One is dated May 21, 1969, to which the Prime Minister habitually refers. It is a letter addressed to the mayor of Montreal, in which the Prime Minister states:
-since the federal government made major contributions for various installations in connection with Expo, and some of these can be used for the Olympic games, I am sure that you will understand that we cannot provide any financial support for the organization of the games or for its publicity.
Next is a letter sent to the president of the International Olympic Committee, dated the same day, in which the Prime Minister said:
The Government of Canada warmly supports the application of the city of Montreal-
I note that in this letter he very carefully did not put a rider or qualification on any support that might be going to the city of Montreal. Apparently, the original of the letter sent to the president of the International Olympic Committee was lost. Later, the Prime Minister conveniently supplied a new original copy so that the Olympic file would be complete. Presumably, in 1969 the Olympic committee put a fair amount of stock in the letter from the Prime Minister. I would also point out that the words used are "financial support". I also refer to their Oxford dictionary definition. On January 15, 1970, the mayor of Montreal wrote to the Prime Minister as follows:
I thank you for giving your official support to our application to host the 1976 Olympic summer games.
I wish to refer to what is recorded in Hansard during this period. On January 22, 1970, the then parliamentary secretary to the minister of consumer and corporate affairs said, as recorded at page 2729 of Hansard:
Montreal did not request direct financial assistance and therefore no commitment has been given to them . . .
Montreal will be seeking indirect financial support under either existing legislation or legislation that might exist in the future concerning urban renewal and public housing.
I emphasize that nowhere did Mr. Drapeau speak about future legislation being restructed to urban renewal and public housing. On March 17, 1970, as recorded at page 5111 of Hansard, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) as to what role the federal government is playing in assisting both Vancouver and Montreal is their Olympic bids, the Prime Minister said:
-this is a rather complicated and lengthy question to answer ... But until a decision is taken on the Olympics I do not think it is useful to make any further statements.
Olympic Bill
It is interesting to note that three years later in this House, on May 10 last, in answer to a similar question by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbak-er) the Prime Minister indicated that it was still a very complicated question and he felt the right hon. member for Prince Albert could not understand it. On May 20, 1970, as recorded at page 7105 of Hansard, documents relating to the Olympic games were tabled by the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Sharp). On May 11, 1971, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Maclnnis), the Prime Minister replied:
In the case of Montreal it was that we were not prepared to assist financially in the organization and carrying out of the Olympics.
It is at this point in the tabled documents that I find an interesting letter from the mayor of Montreal to the Prime Minister in which the mayor requests that the services of His Excellency Roger Rousseau be made available to the Olympic organizing committee. He states it would not be necessary to announce the appointment before February, 1972, but that it would be desirable to obtain consent during the next few weeks. Shortly thereafter, as reported in Hansard at page 109 on February 22, 1972, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated in answer to a question:
There has been no request for financial assistance from Montreal for the 1976 Olympic Games. On the contrary, the city has always assured us that the games would not cost a cent to the federal government and we have always thought the city would keep its word.
On March 29 of the same year, as reported at page 1261 of Hansard, the Prime Minister said, again in answer to a question, that it had been agreed to both sides that the very substantial contribution made by the federal government at the time of Expo was sufficient, and that no special contribution was contemplated by the federal government for the games. At page 1262 he said:
There is not special contribution contemplated by the federal government for the games.
Yet we find that on November 25, 1971, the Prime Minister had sent a letter to the mayor replying to the November 4, 1971, letter and saying:
The Canadian government gladly agrees to make available to you the services of Mr. Rousseau ... It seems logical to me that Mr. Rousseau's salary should continue to be absorbed by the federal government after he assumes his new duties.
I understand that his salary of $30,000 per year is still being paid by the federal government. On August 15, 1972, we find a further letter from the Prime Minister to the mayor in which he states:
The Government of Canada cannot help but be concerned about the international implications of a project such as the Olympic
games.
He went on to say his officials had indicated that there could be a deficit. Generally, the letter expresses concern as to what was taking place in Montreal and how the Olympic expenditures were to be financed. I then find Mr. Rousseau, Chairman and Commissioner General, writing three letters to the Prime Minister, dated November 17, 1972, in which he attempts to clarify three points, namely, the question of the coinage, the question of the stamps and the question of the lottery. He says his committee would like the Prime Minister to authorize and prepare federal
5996


Olympic Bill
legislation to make it possible to do the coin issue, etc. He felt it would make sufficient profit, based upon the experience, in similar circumstances, of Germany, to cover expenses. On parliament's return, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose), the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) said, as reported in Hansard of January 9, 1973, at page 88:
Mr. Speaker, the position of the federal government has not changed from that stated by the Prime Minister in the House some time ago.
Then there is a very interesting letter dated January 20, 1973, from Mr. Rousseau which reads as follows:
I felt it would be useful to review briefly the financial thinking which has always accompanied the various developments relative to the Olympic games.
He says the committee hopes to have recourse to all existing and future legislation and believes it is now imperative that a decision be made and that, to use his words, "this delay cannot be further prolonged." Then he said:
The procedures to follow have also been largely studied with persons authorized, respectively, by the Postmaster General and the Minister of Supply (summer and fall of 1972). They are easy, realistic and effective.
On January 18 we find the Minister of State for Urban Affairs saying there had been some requests of a nonfinancial nature from the organizing committee. He went on to admit that the non-financial items concerned coins, stamps, and things of that sort. He may call them nonfinancial, but that is not the way the Oxford dictionary defines them.
On January 25, in answer to a question by my right hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), the Prime Minister again stated the federal government would not make any special financial aid available to Montreal. In fact, he said, Mayor Drapeau's statements had confirmed his understanding that there was no commitment nor any request that the federal government make any special contribution available for the holding of the games. It is particularly interesting to note that on January 23 the Prime Minister had written to Mayor Drapeau stating, in light of Mr. Rousseau's letter to him of January 20, 1973:
My colleagues and I are greatly concerned about the assumptions which appear to have been made as to the extent of the federal government services which would be provided.
The Prime Minister said it would not be prudent to accede to any "request for federal. . . revenue schemes . .. such as Olympic Coins" without knowing how costs are going to be covered without direct federal involvement. The Prime Minister's concern apparently arose after the Rousseau letter to which I have referred. I would point out that in answering questions, the Prime Minister referred to the fact that he had received a letter from Mr. Rousseau from which he was satisfied that the Montreal group understood the federal position, though he had sent the letter on January 23 stating that he was alarmed. He then asked for guarantees with respect to financial responsibility in case a deficit should arise.
In this connection, three letters have been tabled, one from the Prime Minister of Quebec, one from Mayor Drapeau and one from Mr. Rousseau. In effect, these letters state: If you give us the cash we shall not come against

you for any future deficit. Each of the three letters contained a proviso that unless the federal government agreed to give the net proceeds from the coinage and the stamp issues, the federal government would presumably be required to cover any deficit. I was pleased to hear the President of Treasury Board agree, in answer to a question by me, that he would secure from these three gentlemen an assurance that upon the passage of this bill they would at least recognize that the provisos they mentioned in their letters of January 31 and February 1 have been met by the federal government.
A financial analysis was produced by the government on January 31 in which it was indicated that the deficit might amount to $172 million. It was also pointed out that of a total projected budget for the Olympics of $310 million, the cost of the main arena complex would amount to some $182 million. This is, of course, a major portion of the projected cost, and I would point out that the convertible roof for the arena is not even required as far as the Olympics are concerned.
a (1530)
Coming back to Hansard, in spite of this type of correspondence, the Prime Minister stuck to his story on January 29. Again, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte), the Prime Minister said that the Olympics would not cost the Canadian government a penny. He went on to state, on January 31, at page 831:
-we are simply waiting for some valid assurance not only from a political point of view but from a legal point of view that the Canadian taxpayer will not be the backer in the final analysis.
As has been said, he did receive three letters which, from a legalistic point of view, really say nothing. They simply say that provided the government does certain things, namely, give the Olympic corporation the cash, it will not hold the government responsible for any resulting deficit. In spite of that, on February 2, against a deadline of February 3 when a presentation had to be made in Europe to the International Olympic Committee, he indicated finally that he was satisfied to go ahead with some legislation. That brings us to today. Perhaps I should touch upon one other point. It is interesting to note that on May 10, in answer to what I thought was a very relevant and direct question by the right hon. member for Prince Albert, the Prime Minister gave what I felt was an extremely misleading answer. The question by the right hon. member for Prince Albert is found at page 3611 and reads as follows:
Does it not amount in fact to the people of Canada having to put up, because they will not receive the benefit of the coinage, some $200 million by indirect instead of direct contribution?
The Prime Minister answered:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to the question is no, but 1 think the fact that it was asked proves, indeed, that the complexity of the question is not understood by the right hon. gentleman.
I think what I have related is an unfortunate tale to have to relate to this House. It is difficult to understand how the Prime Minister of a country like Canada could so systematically attempt to create the impression he is not going to contribute to a project, that he is not in any way going to give financial assistance or special aid, yet does exactly that. I believe there is an answer owing by the


Prime Minister to the country. My point is that this is not a question of whether the Olympics is good or bad, or whether Montreal should receive this type of assistance but, rather, it is a question as to whether it is right for any government to be so deceitful about participation in a plan. At some stage do they not admit that they had planned for a significant period of time to do exactly what we have under consideration today?
As I said at the beginning, I believe as members of this House we have to accept reality. We have been led into a situation which is unfortunate. It sets a precedent that I feel will be repeated. In fact, if we read the letter from Mr. Rousseau we find he points out that as one of the advantages of his scheme is that it can be used to finance all kinds of various projects throughout the country he referred to the coinage seigniorage scheme.
We must accept the fact that our Prime Minister got us into this spot. If he wanted to make a grant for the Olympics in Montreal, I wish he had had the courage to say so by introducing whatever estimate he wanted in this House. It is my belief he would have received general support. He did not choose that route, and now having committed us in the name of Canada, we in the opposition had little alternative but to review the provisions of this bill in an effort to determine, by questioning the various representatives who appeared before the committee, what in fact they planned. In that regard I must say most of us were disturbed with the lack of planning that had gone into this matter.
I was pleased that our members were able to propose and have accepted six significant amendments which now appear in the bill before us today. One of these amendments put a limit on the number of coins that may be issued, the limit being set at $450 million. The amendment also limited the maximum amount that may be turned over to the Olympic corporation. It is $260 million. The amendments also require that there be a six months' reporting to this House concerning coinage and related matters, and that if 60 members of the House so desire, they may have the matter debated in the House and referred to the committee.
The amendments dealt with two very great discrepancies in the bill. The first is the fact that the Government of Canada could have been in the position, with the original wording of the bill, to have to issue coinage at a net consideration, which would have resulted in the coinage selling for less than face value. We now have a provision in one of our amendments which prevents that. We have a further provision that ensures that there cannot be side deals, indirect concessions, bonuses or kickbacks, whatever you like to call them, which would have the effect of allowing some persons to buy these coins at a discount.
We also have an amendment which specifically spells out the term "philatelic products" to make sure these are better defined. Finally, there is a provision which requires the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) to call in any coins if he feels there is a circulation problem. As long as the Olympic corporation is in operation when the coins are called in, we have an assurance from the President of the Treasury Board and from representatives who appeared before the committee that a charge-back would be made
Olympic Bill
against the Olympic corporation to cover any net loss as a result of the call-back of the coins.
There was one point that came up subsequent to the committee hearings. We have heard rumours that the Olympic organizers are contemplating the issue of privately minted coinage which might appear to be Olympic coinage. I have taken this matter up with the President of the Treasury Board, who has assured me that he will see to it that this type of coinage will not be issued if it would in any way result in confusion within or outside Canada between legal Canadian Olympic coinage and Olympic coinage which has no value as legal tender.
In short, I believe the committee has made the best of a poor situation. It is unfortunate that something which should be a great national event, the 1976 summer Olympics, has been the subject of this indirect and deceitful type of financing. I see no reason why this nation could not openly finance any project that this or any provincial parliament felt desirable, yet for reasons known only to the Prime Minister and the government they have systematically attempted to mislead the House and the public concerning their true intent. It was not necessary. I hope no government in Canada will stoop so low again. But faced with the reality, as we are today, I feel we have no alternative but to support the bill. However, I would emphasize that we should support it as amended.

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the bill under consideration was introduced in the House, all parties, I think, had the opportunity to meet with His Worship Mayor Jean Drapeau, as well as the Commissioner General for the Olympic games, His Excellency, Mr. Rousseau. When they came to Ottawa, they met with representatives of practically all parties. I personally received them in my office, where I was told that even the New Democratic members supported their project.
When Mr. Drapeau came to Ottawa with Mr. Rousseau, both unfolded their project for the Olympics, and I think they seemed responsible people who were conversant with this matter. After having set forth their self-financing project, they asked for assistance from Ottawa. They did not come to beg from Ottawa funds that would be taken out of the federal treasury itself to be spent in Montreal. They came to suggest a plan studied by experts, and designed to ensure the funding of the Olympics.
Now, Bill C-196 mentions three projects: first, a national lottery, which would be held in all provinces; secondly, the issue of postal stamps which would enable the City of Montreal or COJO to make 2-cent profit per stamp, and thirdly, the issue of commemorative Olympic coins designed for collectors and which would be on sale throughout the world.
Yesterday, I heard the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) say that this would be a complete fiasco. He based his argument on this fiasco of Canada's centennial. But, Mr. Speaker, there is no possible comparison between the centennial which was a national celebration and in no way an international event as the Olympic Games will be, when we will greet people from all countries. As regards Canada's centennial, the hon. member for Timiskaming said that we had, I think, sold 3,500,000 coins and that the
5998


Olympic Bill
Olympic Games would require the coinage of 65 million coins.
Everyone knows, Mr. Speaker-if they do not, I do-that following the centennial, we have received orders for coins and we had all sorts of trouble getting any. We ran short of series, for instance, that were being asked. I got countless telephone calls and letters asking me how to go about getting those Canadian centennial commemorative coins.
In Germany, during the last Olympic Games, there was also a shortage of those coins and I believe the Olympic Games authorities, the mayor of Montreal and Mr. Rousseau went to Europe and here and there throughout the world to determine whether it might be possible to sell those coins to collectors and the general public. Mayor Drapeau tells us it might be possible to finance the Olympic Games through the sale of coins minted on that occasion. So, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the Olympic Games constitute, for Montreal and the whole country, an excellent means of acquainting millions of people throughout the world with Canada.
In 1967, 52 million persons went to Expo. They stimulated commerce and encouraged Canadians in general, but especially Montrealers, Torontonians and westerners. We took advantage of our trip to Montreal to visit Winnipeg, Edmonton, Calgary and Vancouver, and I think that the Olympic Games will provide us with a similar opportunity.
We hear a lot about the losses resulting from Expo 67 in Montreal, but nobody mentions the revenue it provided, the economic development it fostered in Canada. Before Expo, Mr. Speaker, we did not have the highway system we have now; there was no subway in Montreal. Thanks to Expo, Montreal developed remarkably. By way of consequence, this helped even Toronto and Winnipeg. Even the riding of the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) may have benefited. Mr. Speaker, if we consider only the liabilities and do not take into consideration how it benefited the people, our assessment is all wrong. Have we taken into account, for instance, the income tax paid by the citizens of Montreal and other Canadians who benefitted from Expo? That was never done. No one ever said either what Canada gained through income tax. The same thing will happen with the Olympic Games in 1976.
I realize that the possibilities would be greater if we had another system for financing the Olympic Games, which, whether we like it or not, will in the end have their justification. Vancouver had applied for the Olympic Games. Denver, in the U.S., and other cities in the rest of the world, including Moscow, made the same application. Why? Because it is an opportunity to make the city and the country where the Games are held better known.
When I visit France and ask the French if they know where Canada is situated, they answer they think it is close to China, which is far from the truth. If we invite them and if they come to visit us, they will find out that we are quite far from China. In fact, we are closer to France than to China.
Mr. Speaker, the Olympic Games will benefit Montreal and the whole of Canada; they will attract visitors from all parts of the world.

This bill deals with a lottery. I am not what they call a gambler, but when one is against lotteries, one does not get any money in his pockets. It is profitable for the one who wins, but many have to chip in, and everybody knows that. Even when lotteries did not exist, people used to gamble. The Mini-Loto, the Super-Loto, Loto-Quebec and all other "lotos" in Quebec bring in profits; people just love to buy tickets. Even the Irish sweepstake operates wonderfully in Canada. I bet the hon. member for Timis-kaming buys tickets for the Irish sweepstake. Instead of buying these tickets and sending his money to Ireland, he will be buying Canadian lottery tickets to finance the Olympic Games or part of them. He will thus promote something in this country. But yesterday, he spoke against the lottery-not against the Irish sweepstake which is not there to help the financing of the Montreal Olympic Games.
And now, the postage stamps. Nobody will be required to buy them. But if we do buy some, two cents per stamp will go to COJO. But we will not have to buy any. We will still be able to use the postage stamps showing the Western wheat fields or those in honour of Sir John A. Macdonald, at the regular price. But stamp collectors will buy a lot of those on the occasion of the Montreal Olympic Games.
If the hon. member for Timiskaming or his colleagues of the NDP do not want to buy any stamps, let them not buy any, but let them not prevent others from buying some if they wish to do so. It seems to me it is as simple as that. And, at the same time, we help the Olympic Games.
Concerning the coins, they are afraid too many will be issued; the hon. member said yesterday "out of a windbag-or something like that", coins based on nothing. But those who will be buying coins will indirectly contribute $2, I think, to COJO. These people will keep the coins and the money now in circulation will not be devalued. Those who will have them are not going to take anything from anyone. However, these coins will constitute a souvenir for their purchasers all over the world.
During centennial year coins were selling at higher cost than their value. We bought them just the same; this has not thrown the Canadian economy out of kilter. My set is at home and I am not using it. So it does not create inflation at all. And all those who have kept those coins obviously do not use them; so this is not what creates inflation or unbalances the economy of a country like Canada.
But the important point, the capital point, Mr. Speaker, is that the Olympics will be held in Canada, in the City of Montreal. Instead of objecting to it, we should with one voice congratulate the mayor of Montreal who brought them here. He really did and God knows how he devoted himself, travelled, spent his time, his money, everything, to put Montreal and Canada on the map.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, even at some cost, it is worth to make Canada known and to show the entire world that we too, a small nation of 20 million inhabitants, can hold the Olympic Games which, I think, will attract millions of people and enable Canada to show her great hospitality, her intellectual, physical, and material development, while the nations that do not know Canada today will have this unique opportunity of making themselves known.


That is why my colleagues and myself strongly support the request of Mayor Drapeau and the Organizing Committee of tfre Olympic Games. I suggest that the members stop opposing a bill that will enable Canada to be better known and have a stronger voice not only from the economic point of view, but also from the Olympic Games point of view, and to show that we, as every other nation, are interested in sports.
We saw not so long ago the Russian hockey team give us a surprise here in Canada, with regard to our national sport; we were almost beaten by people whom we thought were second rate. We found out that people learn how to play hockey outside Canada, and we learned it the hard way.
But now, in turn, we can show the whole world and our own people in Montreal that we are not only hockey players, but that we can train in other sports that our young athletes are first rate, enterprising, that they have achieved something. Those young people, I am convinced, will thank Mayor Drapeau of Montreal, Mr. Rousseau and COJO, and will be grateful to the Canadian Parliament for Bill C-196 which provides for the self-financing of the Olympic Games, not at our expense, but through a sensible program.

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by reassuring the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) that my party is not opposed to the Olympics, nor is it opposed to sports generally. Had he read the remarks I made on June 28, he would know that I dealt with a number of the matters that he raised. Certainly I am as concered as he is about the success of the games. I will be as proud as he and all Canadians were of Expo. That is not the point of the argument. If that is what it appears to him, then he missed the point.
I was very interested in the remarks of the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). He spent a great deal of time attacking the irresponsibility of my political party, pointing out with a great deal of force and, I suppose, with a bit of logic some inconsistencies in our position. He interrupted the debate yesterday to suggest that we had somehow switched our position since early February. That is true: we have. That was admitted by me when I spoke on second reading on June 28, less than a month ago. I suppose it is the height of egotism to quote myself, but I said on that date:
We recognize also that our opposition to Bill C-196 is a departure from the position I, personally, took last February in my response to the Prime Minister's statement on motions, which at that time was intended to assure the House that any deficit accruing from the games would not be borne by the federal government.
I make no apology for this. I think we would be irresponsible to pursue blindly a course we felt was wrong merely because in a quick response to a statement on motions we committed ourselves to God knows what deficit, approximately $500 million, which is as much as we spend per year on post-secondary education in this country, now to be spent on a two-week extravaganza, a two-week carnival of sweat. I hope my attitude would be no different if the same kind of financing scheme were dreamed up to finance the games kind be they held in
Olympic Bill
Montreal, Vancouver or any other city. Let us get that straight.
I think the hon. member for York-Simcoe did an excellent job on the committee. Bui he was trapped. I realize he was trapped because a very prominent member of his party had pretty well committed them to what I think is a bad deal. As a matter of fact, his concluding remarks indicated that it was a bad deal and that they were going to attempt to make the best of it. The first response was to attack the irresponsibility of my party. I reject that, Mr. Speaker. What it exhibits to me is the well known psychological phenomenon associated with guilt, known as reversal formation-blame somebody else for your own problems.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe said that we have to accept reality. That sounds like a quotation from my words of February 6, but I no longer agree with that; and I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that some other places no longer agree with it either. Denver, Colorado, did not agree with the winter Olympics: the population turned it down. And it was not to cost $500 million or $750 million, but a mere $3'/2 million. That figure is pale in comparison with the amount we are considering. My party was the only one consistently to oppose this bill on second reading as vigorously and as vociferously as we could, and through committee as well. We intend to vote against it on third reading. I am only sorry that we were not here to vote against it in a standing vote on second reading.
My colleagues, members of the government and those members of the opposition who are locked in-they might as well be members of the government-on this issue have a right to ask why we oppose the bill. I will tell those hon. members why. I cannot help their embarrassment; that is their own problem and has nothing to do with me. I think it would be fair to say that our position on this matter is based on the following grounds. First of all, we take the position that if the Olympic games are worth funding at all, they are worth funding properly through an outright federal grant. If they are not worth funding that way, then they are not worth funding by any method, especially by a gimmicky, half-baked assortment of coins, stamps and lotteries.
When we spoke on February 6 we had no idea how the funding was to be done, nor had anybody else. Nobody knows, not even the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) or the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet). About 80 per cent of the Olympics is to be financed by this gimmick. We think that is ludicrous, patent nonsense. But 80 per cent of the Olympic financing depends on the coin scheme alone. Nothing has convinced me or my party that a deficit can be avoided.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has assured us that there will be no additional request for federal support. The mayor of Montreal and the Premier of Quebec have assured him of that. But if there is a deficit and the federal government does not pick it up, who does? The deficit will be borne by those Canadians who live in Montreal and Quebec, those people who by and large have an income of about half the national average but who have twice the


Olympic Bill
unemployment experienced in other provinces. We are going to ask those Canadians to pick up the deficit.

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
My colleague says that we will do it eventually. I would rather do it now. If it is worth while, let us do it now; let us not get ourselves involved in this kind of nonsense. The analysts working for the President of the Treasury Board predicted at the committee hearings a deficit of $150 million to $170 million. At that time I asked the minister whose analysis he would be more inclined to accept, that of COJO or that of his own department. I think he is loyal to his staff; he replied that he preferred the response of his own officials.
We are committed to a downhill run with such momentum that it cannot be stopped. Well, Denver stopped it. I do not think the Olympics necessarily need be stopped, but I think we need a much better financing foundation. Members of the opposition are not reassured at all, but they are muzzled. They have the same misgivings they have always had, but they are committed.
According to the Postmaster General, this scheme contemplates the minting of $450 million worth of gold and silver coins over the next four years, roughly half of which are to be sold overseas. All the silver coins circulated in Canada since confederation have amounted to only $317 million, according to the master of the Mint. We are going to put all that extra coinage into circulation, which will mean the importation of 51 million troy ounces of silver in a world desperately short of silver for industrial purposes. We are going to make souvenir coins and thus bury the silver after we have spent time taking it out of the ground. This is legal tender which will go into circulation. It will cause trouble to everybody, including COJO. This is my first reservation.
My second reservation is that the priorities are all wrong. I am sorry that the hon. member for Temis-camingue has left the Chamber, because he made reference to something which I should like to correct. We feel that the spending priorities in this connection are all wrong. The amount involved is $500 million. Somebody will say it is really only $350 million, but the Germans started out at $152 million and ended up at $700 million. Also, on second reading the President of the Treasury Board said there could be some escalating costs over the four years, so I think $500 million is reasonably conservative. One per cent of $500 million-that is, $5 million- would build 100 community swimming pools in the city of Montreal for the youth whom the hon. member for Temis-camingue is so concerned about. They are desperately short of recreation facilities in Montreal and could use 100 outdoor pools, not necessarily of Olympic size. That is why we question the spending priorities.
I mentioned earlier that Mr. Drapeau and Mr. Bourassa would pick up the deficit. But how do we know that either of these hon. gentlemen will be in office in 1976? We have no assurance of that. These gentlemen are honourable in all ways, but we do not know whether they will still be in office in 1976. We are going to be asked to help with the deficit, and I for one want to help; make no mistake about that. Across the river is the city of Hull. For the last ten years that city has been trying to get an indoor swimming

pool. The city officials recently cancelled a $12 million recreation complex on the ground that there is no money for it. They need $12 million. The Olympics want $500 million.
Let us for the moment forget about pollution, slums, traffic and problems such as providing plumbing and preventing illiteracy in Montreal. The point is that there is no money in the budget for the city of Hull. They go to the province and are told there is no money. They go to the federal government and are told there is no money. Other communities across the country are in the same difficulty. If they want to play ice hockey and ask for money to build a rink, they are told, sorry, but there is no money from the federal government; why not do it with volunteers? If they need a stadium for a track team, the answer is that there is no money. They go to Sports Canada who say, sorry, we are not in the business of capital financing; we can help with coaching, but not with money.
~
Yet we are to spend $500 million in this area. Why could we not spend $500 million to meet Canadian recreational needs, raising the money as the money for the Olympics is to be raised? Why should we not put out special coins in order to supply every community with recreational amenities such as stadiums, community pools and that sort of thing? But no, we do not do that because, we say, we do not have any money. That is nonsense.

speechtext: What about hockey?

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) has mentioned hockey. That is one of the sports at which we do well. Why? Is it because we spend a great deal of money on rinks? No. We are a northern country, and our kids skate on rivers and ponds. Yet in every community kids get up at four o'clock in the morning, with their coaches, because there is not enough ice time to allow them to play during the day. We lack these facilities. If we build stadiums, pools and tracks, I am sure that in ten years we could be as good at other Olympic sports as we are at hockey. That is why we question the kinds of priorities represented by this bill. We are fed up with this attitude of the government.
The Fitness and Amateur Sport Act has been in existence since 1962. Since that time some $60 million has been budgeted for the purpose of fitness and amateur sport in Canada. In the last ten years only half of the allocated budget has been taken up. Every year $5 million has been devoted tc this area, which means that roughly $60 million could have been spent. Yet only about $30 million has been taken up. That being so, why is the allocation to be raised to $9.8 million this year? Some people are a bit cynical and suspicious about these things. The Fitness and Amateur Sport Act entitles the government to make special arrangements with certain provinces, so there may be more to this iceberg than the tip we see at the moment. I realize that is "insinnuendo".

I meant insinuation. As well, we do not have all the necessary information. The President of the Trea-


sury Board assured us that each province would get its fair share of the $9.8 million, and I have no reason to doubt that. The act entitles the provinces to that. My third misgiving is this. We were denied information in committee. speechtext: They were in bed with the Liberals.

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
I am not worried about that; that is not my concern. They are a party of principle, and I wish they would back their convictions with their votes. I do not know what brought about the change of heart. I only know one thing, that the committee was absolutely deadlocked on Thursday two weeks ago. When we came back, by Tuesday night all the amendments went flying through. I do not know how it happened. I think the Conservatives were trying to make parliament work. Anyway, all the Conservative motions were passed.
The Conservatives tried to make a good deal this afternoon of their putting this and that through in committee, yet they did not ever question the principle of the bill. They took what I termed the cornflakes approach, accepting the prize in the cornflakes package. That was their approach to funding the Olympics. They were not against the bill. They limited the total expenditure package to $450 million and wanted to limit the income to $240 million. I
Olympic Bill
do not know why they were interested in limiting the net returns on these sales.
Hon. members to my right will demand reports in future, and want to include in the bill what I term a 60-member review clause. They stole that idea from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), who introduced it in connection with the corporations bill. Those hon. members know a lot about corporations. In any event, they did not really question the principle of the bill, and it is the principle that my party attempted to question. I want to make that clear.
We must not forget that we were told this scheme will not cost the federal government any money. Let me remind hon. members that the basic cost to Canadians, the seed money, if you like, to start this venture is $100 million. There is about $50 million for housing, $27 million for security and $25 million for broadcasting. If you add the seigniorage for $250 million which the government will not get from the sale of these coins, that brings you pretty close to $350 million. So don't suggest this will not cost us anything, because that is misleading. Such suggestions mislead the public and I think the public will wake up to this one of these days.
In the second reading debate my party was concerned, as were other hon. members, about the lack of concrete planning. The Postmaster General and the President of the Treasury Board admitted before the committee that they did not know how things would work out. They suggested that in the matter of the coins we are breaking new ground. They were in the dark and did not know what would happen. They are probably pushing on like lemmings, to be drowned in the sea of their own optimism. I do not mind so long as they do not take the Canadian people with them. I would object to that because it would be most unfair.
My party is concerned in case the Olympic village funded by Central Mortgage and Housing becomes a ghetto of the future. We know that at least 70,000 citizens of Montreal back the Green Space committee which sent in a petition objecting to the present location of the village. I know that Dr. Goldbloom, the municipal affairs minister of Quebec, is also concerned.

speechtext: They should fill a lake.

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
I don't know if they will fill a lake or chop an island in two. In any event, my party is also concerned about the $27 million worth of armed forces and police security which will turn Montreal into an armed camp for two weeks in 1976. The security personnel will not be there to protect us from the citizens of Montreal but they will be required, hon. members may agree, if they recall what happened in Munich and in Mexico City. Security forces are needed because people like the Black September gang use these large spectaculars to make some kind of point which their warped minds can understand but mine cannot. Hon. members know this will happen: They know the place will be an armed camp. We would be concerned about these things happening, whether the Olympics were being held in Vancouver, Toronto or Halifax. It does not have anything to do with the location; that is irrelevant. It is still a bad deal.


Olympic Bill
It has not escaped the notice of many members, including some members opposite, that leading editorial and sports writers have applauded the stand of the New Democratic Party. This is not confined to English language newspapers such as the Globe and Mail and the Star. It includes such prestigious French language journals as La Presse and Le Devoir. These editorials in themselves do not make the NDP position right. However, I think it is. Truth is not a matter of how many people believe in something. The fact that we have this type of support indicates that the stand we have taken, regardless of its linguistic overtones, is right.
I do not know how much time I have left. It is fair to ask what our party proposes as alternatives. There are basically two alternatives. We want a less expensive Olympics.

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
At the moment, there are perhaps only five cities in the world that could host an Olympics of this magnitude. This rules out many countries such as the developing countries of Africa and Asia. They cannot afford it. We would like a less extravagant Olympics. We are prepared to openly grant up to $200 million. We do not want it to be financed in the same way as paying off a church mortgage.
The second point is that, for reasons of security, we feel the Olympic games should be dispersed among the cities of central Canada such as Quebec City, Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto. Facilities already exist in these places. There are college campuses with dormitories and stadiums. It is not necessary to build a stadium costing $178 million which will only be for the benefit of the NFL or the Expos baseball team.
I regret we have to stand alone on this issue. There has been excellent criticism from the party to my right, and by the hon. member for Matane (Mr. De Bane). I am sorry the misgivings and criticisms voiced have gone virtually unheeded. I am sorry the hon. member for Matane could not get the help of his colleagues on this matter. This event will not do anything for the average citizen of Montreal. However, he will have to pay for it. He probably will not even attend the games. He will be able to watch it on television, but he could do that if they were located in outer Mongolia.
Companies will probably purchase tickets in large blocks to be given to their friends, as is the case with hockey games and the National Arts Centre. They give these tax free gifts to the boys for promotional purposes. The average Canadians will be lined up from the Ottawa River to Vancouver in an attempt to get tickets.
I share the hopes of many Liberals and Conservatives that I am dead wrong on this question. I hope I am dead wrong.

speechtext: I just hope you are dead.

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) is not serious in his hope for my instant mortality, or is it immortality? I certainly feel the same toward him. Maybe a few severe chest pains would help him see reality and
[Mr. Rose.)
how close we are to being involved in this ludicrous nonsense.
All Canadians were proud of Expo. I am sure they will be proud of the Olympic games. We agree on that. However, that is not the point. We do not like the method of funding the games. In spite of the Treasury Board's analysis, I hope the estimates of the President of the Treasury Board and the Postmaster General, who are sitting benignly surrounded by silver coins, are correct and mine are wrong. It would be a pleasure to hop out of my cozy bed and have my place taken by members of the official opposition on this: it would be a nice change.
For my efforts I have been called a racist and a bigot. An hon. member called me something else which is not parliamentary. These things may have some relevance, but I do not think anything in our record warrants that kind of appellation being applied to me or my party. I regret the government saw fit to include only Francophones on this committee. I think the linguistic overtones were enhanced by that decision, and I am sorry about it. Recently, the CBC took a poll with regard to the acceptance of the Montreal Olympics. It showed that 80 per cent of the people in the province of Quebec are in favour of the Olympics. When a second question was asked, whether they would be in favour of the Olympics if there was a deficit, 80 per cent were against.
I would love to have been in cabinet and overheard the discussions on this bill. I hope the optimist will be accurate and the pessimists will be wrong. If we are going to have the Olympics, we want them to be a success. We have outlined our objections in detail. I am sorry we did not have a more searching examination in committee. I am sorry we had to be dependent upon the gentlemen I mentioned earlier. However, I feel we have at last had some opportunity to examine this question and, on the basis of that examination, to expose its faults. On the basis of that examination we are voting against the bill.

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will speak very briefly for fear of being unjustly accused of unduly delaying the passing of this bill.
Now that we are about to dispose of the motion that the bill on the 1976 Olympic Games be read the third time, we must not once again forget that since the end of the 1972 Munich Games the whole world, and especially the younger generation, have an appointment in Montreal in 1976. I would like the most incredulous of us to know that, in accordance with the spirit of the Olympic movement, many developing countries will be participating in the 1976 Games. We will see on the podium the greatest champions in all the disciplines and undoubtedly athletes from underprivileged nations who, because of their achievements and their long training, will find the required energy and courage to have faith in the building of their countries. And would it be only for them, the most sceptical among us should consider and reconsider their judgment about the opportunity and advisability of holding these Olympic Games.
As far as I am concerned, to reiterate what I stated clearly during the debate on second reading, I believe in the Olympic Games. I believe in the 1976 Montreal Olym-


pic Games and I cannot accept the pessimistic utterances of some NDP members.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that we must commend however the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) who tacitly at least did not seem to endorse the views of some of his colleagues and did not readily yield to the temptation to disparage Montreal, its mayor, Quebec and the Olympic Games.
In the same breath, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be fair to single out the Leader of the Social Credit (Mr. Caouette) who this afternoon in an enthusiastic and vigorous speech expressed his deep feelings about the Olympic Games and has undoubtedly impressed all members by clearly saying what most of us believe at the bottom of our hearts.
Mr. Speaker, the 1976 games will leave in Montreal and throughout the country some new infrastructure components and more particularly a genuine infrastructure for amateur sport and physical fitness.
Because of the Games a stadium and related facilities will be built capable of accommodating in addition to the professional baseball, football, soccer, and other teams, record crowds coming from all corners of the world to participate in various conventions, world-wide rallies which will benefit the whole country.
Because of the Games and for the very benefit of its industrial and commercial institutions, or even for the benefit of any one of its levels of government, severely schooled in new challenges, Canada will have acquired modern techniques and human skills.
Because of the Games, and somewhat as a result and consequence of the 1967 World Exhibition, people or social groups from Panet Street in Montreal or Grande-Allee in Quebec City, from Matane or Saint-Hyacinthe, as well as Halifax or Vancouver will have taken a liking to opening up to the world and, as one could say, to having "windows fully opened on the world." They will have tried to make our problems, our inspirations known to others but also they will have learned to better appreciate the problems, inspirations and accomplishments of others and thanks to those international exchanges, a new spirit will evolve, a spirit that will inevitably have the effect of inspiring in its wake the development of elements of that new cultural, social and economic substructure and even the setting up of facilities likely to increase our means and add to the well-being of the community.
Because of the Games, Mr. Speaker, the people of Montreal who already have on Mount Royal one of the greatest natural green parks in the world will have recovered more than half of notorious ViauPark, the use of which, unfortunately, until now was restricted to a very few privileged people, who even at that had to be golfers. And perhaps here again, Mr. Speaker, the Games might have the consequential effect of increasing in Montreal and elsewhere in the country the number of green areas and above all the number of those who will truly want to use them for purposes of pure relaxation or as a place to do their physical fitness exercises.
Olympic Bill
Thanks to these games-and this is most important and certainly will be available to all citizens of our large country-a permanent substructure in the area of amateur sport and physical fitness will be set up throughout Canada. No doubt it will be from this long term result that we will be able to judge the opportunity and the wisdom of holding the Olympic Games in Canada in 1976.
Mr. Speaker, we live in a country where our professional sport is as much out of our control as our economy. I am convinced that with the representations made by our young people, the games of 1976 will force us, after the event to get out of this kind of amateurism of ours, in the area of amateur sport, an amateurism which is revealed by the absence of a real government policy on sports and spare time activities, by frictions in this area at the different provincial and federal jurisdiction levels, by the reluctance of the educational world, unfortunately by the lack of specialized instructors and highly qualified trainers.
Between now and 1976 the Games will at last give Canada as a whole the opportunity to discover a new kind of motivation and a reinforced determination to secure in the area of sports and spare time activities the qualified resources which will remain with us after 1976. These resources, strengthened by the fire of the Olympic flame, will enable young people from Point St. Charles or from other districts in Montreal, who live in houses without running water or bathtub, or shower, or whose father is unemployed, to have other option than drug or the lane "macadam". They will be encouraged to throw themselves wholeheartedly into pole jumping, javelin throwing or what have you. Mr. Speaker, I want to say here that before 1976 and afterwards, we will have to combine our efforts at the different levels of government to solve the unemployment problem, to check the constant increase in the cost of living, in food prices in particular, pharmaceuticals, clothing and housing. We will have to ensure that every Canadian, in Montreal and elsewhere, enjoy normal health conditions and, on a broader scope, that they all have equal opportunities to develop in life. But-and everyone without exception will likely admit it-they were not matters brought forth by the spirit of Bill C-196 as such and which it could solve or had to solve. For once, Mr. Speaker, politics can serve sport instead of using it. Therefore, I urge all my colleagues to grasp this occasion firmly.
Given the 1976 Games, and this Bill C-196, let politics have a chance to serve sports. It can and must serve them, especially considering the fact that amateur sports, and even more so the Olympic Games, have a bearing on all the great problems that condition the future of our civilization: youth, the use of leisure, urbanization, environment and even medical research.
There is no doubt that resounding lessons, that will benefit all Canadians, will be learned because the Olympic Games will be held in Canada. Mr. Speaker, the social impact of the 1976 Games, a few aspects of which I have just pointed out, deserves our attention, but we should not forget their economic impact as well, which will be measured mainly by the increased flow of tourists throughout the country, not only while the Games are being held but long afterwards.

Olympic Bill
These are arguments that reach much farther that national pride and international prestige. Those are arguments which, I am convinced, will stir in all Canadians a feeling of solidarity with the 1976 Games, and in that feeling of solidarity, the will to contribute to their success.
Commemorative coins, stamps, a national lottery, will all be as many opportunities for Canadians to say "yes", according to each individual's possibilities, to the 1976 Olympic Games. First, the promoters, then the Canadian people, must discharge their very special responsibility, that of proving to the world that from here on, the Olympic Games will be financially within the reach of the developing countries, whether they be African or Latin American.
In the course of the debate on second reading, as well as in a committee, during the exchanges of information and the introduction of amendments, everybody managed to throw light on and define this bill. Now, on third reading, I have no doubt that in every part of the nation, regardless of political affiliations, through their constant interest, and interventions, hon. members who represent those areas, who represent those political parties, hear testimony today to the national and truly Pan Canadian responsibility of the 1976 Games.
Let us make sure, Mr. Speaker, that once this legislation is passed, it will not become the sole responsibility of the present government, but that of Parliament as a whole and, consequently, let us be in our constituencies the promoters of the 1976 Games for the Canadian people.
Let us inform our constituents of the national challenge of 1976, of the costs of such a challenge, but also of the real and already anticipated benefits. Mr. Speaker, all Canadians, regardless of their province, their mother tongue and their culture, should be proud, as they are, I believe, to see their country be in 1976, the host and the crossroad of a world event which is essentially peaceful.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I make it a point to express a few thoughts on third reading of this very important bill. Since I have always taken an interest in recreational activities, I did not want to miss this opportunity to make a few comments.
On second reading, I have had the opportunity, as a good many other members, to make some comments on the bill designed to finance the Olympic Games of 1976 and, I regretted, of course, the mitigated part taken by the government. I would have hoped that, considering the national character of the games and the national and international participation in these games, Canadians would not hesitate to take the risk of making some profit or incurring deficits, and I realize at the stage of the third reading that while we are considering the possibility of financing the games, we are very careful not to commit ourselves in the event financial problems arise.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I say, as the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) pointed out earlier, if politics serve sports, perhaps the political context badly serves CO JO. I was very pleased to hear the comments of the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe, and I do not question for a moment his interest in the success of these games, not only for the benefit of the province of Quebec

but also for that of all participants, in whatever capacity they act, as spectators or as amateurs.
But I said that the political context could ill serve the interests and the possibilities of success of COJO because we know perfectly well that the government, on the one hand, found it a little embarrassing to open wide its doors to provide more assistance and, on the other, we also know that certain political parties are opposing it for other reasons, in attempting to shift the problem or in assuring themselves that Canadians will not have to pay a penny more that what the bill provides.
But we agree and we accept and we boast to whoever wants to listen that these events will be beneficial, which also constitutes a commitment, I think, by all Canadians, if we recognize-and we all do-the national character of the Olympic Games of 1976.
It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that there has been talks between the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and Mayor Drapeau of Montreal. It is also obvious that, after the elections held last October, it was embarrassing for the government to do more than it does.
It is also obvious that, unfortunately, political interests often take precedence over the interests of society. This has led the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) to say yesterday, on behalf of his party, that he would accept no other financial obligation than those described in the bill before us.
So, I think that, politically speaking, we are trying to protect some regions which would be less favourable than others to these Olympic Games, while we are showing eagerness in saying that those events are a national feature, and since we recognize it, we have to take part in those events and commit ourselves as Canadians.
I certainly deplore the position of the New Democratic Party which persisted in shifting its ground when maintaining that if all those millions were earmarked for housing, sewer services, infrastructures of all kinds, it would readily endorse the bill. We know perfectly well that the Olympic Games will take place, as other members were saying a moment ago, and that there still will be some problems in that area.
Some people are suggesting that the games will be a two-week affair, and that the millions involved are an unacceptable expense for Canadians, particularly if ever Quebecers had to shoulder a deficit as foreseen by the government.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think we solved the issue by shifting the problem. On the contrary, these social or economic problems exist and will continue to exist but it will become possible to do more in the field of leisure as the Olympic Games will arouse a motivation which will last much longer than the two weeks of the games. Some regional and provincial leisure organizations are already in operation. The federation of leisure organization will operate better than ever and after the Olympic events these structures will continue to operate. I think it is an advantage and an honour for Canada to host the games. As Canada is a relatively young country compared with others, I think it will achieve remarkable success as it will have made sensitized not only the federal government but


also provincial governments, municipal organizations and municipalities themselves deeply aware of amateur sports.
Municipalities complain about the lack of necessary institutions, the lack of basic tools, the lack of educators, instructors and trainers. I think the motivation that young and also older people are already getting will prompt to vote the funds which will enable Canadians to improve their physical fitness.
We know the importance of being physically apt in our society today.
Mr. Speaker, no doubt that even if this bill is limited to the financing of the games, quite contradictory views have been expressed in committee and at the second and third reading stages. To come back to the position taken by the New Democratic Party, I do not want to forget the statement made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) following the announcement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about the involvement of the Federal government. Mention was made of it yesterday and I think that it is worth repeating. He said, and I quote: -my party welcomes the statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) today in which he took some trouble to outline the parameters of federal involvement in Canada's first Olympic games. We wish our first Olympic games every possible success as a potentially great moment in the history of our nation.
Since then, we have heard quite different stories. However, I am not at all surprised by the NDP's new position, considering that since last January 4, that party has often changed its mind and made sure that this legislation which might embarrass the government is adopted. I would even go so far as to say that if the Progressive Conservative Party was against this bill, the New Democratic Party would be for it. Mr. Speaker, I do not think that Canadians who have seen members of that party at work since the beginning of the session are very much impressed by their statements.
I regret that they tried to put Mayor Drapeau on trial or tarnish his reputation concerning his administration, because I feel that several political parties would have liked to be able to count on such a popular man with tremendous achievements to his credit. Of course, some people in Montreal will complain about not having such and such a service, but I think that Mayor Drapeau has done one extraordinary thing for Montreal: he put that city on the map so that is better known throughout the world, and the participation that we will witness in 1976 will be beneficial not only to Montreal, but also to all Canadian cities. We will be welcoming important visitors and I think that the economic impact will be worthwhile, because there will be opportunities of inviting people from abroad to come and visit us, and they will leave something as was the case with Expo '67.
Before concluding I would like to talk about the deficit which the government expected. Even if some members of COJO are rather optimistic towards the possibility of a deficit, nevertheless the responsibility of Quebecers should not be ignored. I think we should especially consider that such a situation could occur.
We know the present context and position of Quebec within Canada. Let us imagine for a moment that there will be a deficit and that Quebecers and Montrealers would be solely responsible for it.
