speechtext:
Mr. Gerard Laprise (Abitibi), for Mr. Adrien Lambert (Bellechasse), moved:
That an Order of the House do issue for copies of the contract and all documents relating to a grant by the Department of
26454-16 \

Regional Economic Expansion
Regional Economic Expansion to the newspaper Le Soleil of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank all my hon. colleagues very sincerely for allowing me to move this motion on behalf of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) who had to attend the funerals of one of his brothers, and I take this opportunity to offer him my most heartfelt sympathy.
The motion now before us which I had the honour to move on behalf of the hon. member for Bellechasse has been on the Order Paper since February 21, 1973. It asks that the House order the ministry to issue all the documents relating to a grant offer which has reportedly been made by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion to the Corporation du journal Le Soleil of Quebec City. As this is a motion of public interest, I hope that I shall be supported by all my colleagues, so that the motion may be carried before 6 o'clock.
Mr. Speaker, it is neither on a sudden impulse that we are requesting the issue of these documents nor to satisfy our own curiosity. On the contrary, we aim at enlightening the Canadian people as to the way appropriations which are made available to the various departments are being used.
During recent days, through the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) who made a long statement in the House and through the tabling of a green paper on conflicts of interest of ministers and members of Parliament, the government has tried to reassure the public concerning the honesty of ministers and members of Parliament who are responsible for the administration of public funds.
The government also tried to inform the public about the measures it intends to take to ensure the independence of its members against the economic dictatorship which exerts increasing pressures upon the political power, both at the legislative and executive level.
Lastly, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made a long statement in which he put before Parliament the measures he intends to have accepted in order to prevent conflicts of interest.
Under the rules governing this House, hon. members are given extraordinary privileges based upon the principle of democracy. Among those privileges, there is the right for every member to control funds made available to the various departments of which the minister is responsible to Parliament. Consequently, it is reasonable and normal for a minister to reply to an enquiry made by a member. One may reply that the government set out criteria for the production of such papers that were published on March 15th, 1973. The general principle of those criteria is the following:
General Principle
To enable Members o£ Parliament to secure factual information about the operations of government to carry out their parliamentary duties and to make public as much factual information as possible consistant with effective administration, the protection of the security of the state, rights to privacy and other such matters, government papers, documents and consultant reports should be produced on Notice of Motion for the Production of Papers unless falling within the categories outlined below in which case an exemption is to be claimed from production.

Following that, we find a list of exemptions which I will not read entirely, with the permission of the House. However, I should like to quote section No. 10.
Papers relating to negotiations leading up to a contract until the contract has been executed or the negotiations have been concluded.
That means that the papers could not be tabled as long as negotiations leading up to a contract have not been concluded. In the present case, which is mentioned in the motion, section 10 does not apply, since it is not a matter of pending negotiations prior to a contract. On the contrary, the negotiations ended a long time ago, the agreement was signed and the subsidy granted, since it was the topic of the article published in all the newspapers.
The Department of Regional Economic Expansion was set up by an act of Parliament. Regulations governing the application of that legislation were drawn by senior officials. This department's purpose is to encourage regional economic development by granting special advantages to industries through loans or subsidies. Subsidies can be offered to manufacturing or processing industries which set up, enlarge or modernize their plants in designated areas, or special areas.
Most manufacturing and processing industries are eligible for subsidies except oil refineries, industries transforming minerals into concentrates, and pulp and paper industries.
However, it is stipulated that in some "special areas" subsidies can be granted to industries that are not eligible under the terms of the regional development incentives program. Was that rule applied in the case of Le Soleil mentioned in the motion?
Can printing be considered as a manufacturing or processing operation? If the answer is yes, why can the same not be said of milling industries, which use all types of grains and other products and transform them into cubed feed? Recognizing that grants can be made to a newspaper-whether it be Le Soleil of Quebec or any other- while refusing to grant them to milling enterprises, constitute to my mind a most serious weakness which should be remedied right away.
This reminds me of the case of the Meunerie cooperative de Saint-Fran?ois, which was destroyed by fire. Members of the co-operative have decided to rebuild the millstone factory and to modernize their industry. Eleven jobs have thus been created, but that firm could not benefit from any grant from the Department.
If by subsidizing newspapers we in fact help them to get better organized in order to provide the public with a better quality information and to free them from the obligation to accept any kind of dangerous advertising which gives our children a bad orientation and causes a lot of concern to parents and the authorities in general, at least the government will have a valid argument to justify his policy.
What we are asking for through this motion is simply some information. And as representatives elected by the people and members of Parliament, which is after all the highest authority in this country, it seems that we have a

right to know in detail the arrangements which have been reached concerning the subsidies granted by the executive.
Who will monitor the way in which the taxpayer's money is spent if the government refuses to answer the inquiries of members of this House?
It will be perhaps answered that the Auditor General is responsible for that. I agree; however, my hon. colleagues know quite well that in the last few years the reports of the auditor have been quite severe, but did the government take them into account?
In the notes of the last report of the Auditor General one can read at paragraph 107: "Shared costs under a development contract not verified. Basic documents not released."
Mr. Speaker, even the Auditor General complains about a lack of information due to the unavailability of basic documents.
At page 91 of his last report the Auditor General states in his remarks on the use of funds allocated to local initiative projects, and I quote:
1.	Extensions to the Program from May 31 to June 16, to September 30 and then to November 30, 1972, substantially altered it from a winter job-creating program to one of continuing employment aid.
2.	Contributions were made to projects in circumstances where improvements to privately-owned property were being financed in whole or in part from funds provided under the Program.
And at paragraph 5 one can read:
5. Some project workers were self-employed, such as farmers and fishermen, while others were full-time students. Several instances were noted where individuals received wages from projects while employed elsewhere on a full-time basis.
Mr. Speaker, all this to say that in addition to the Auditor General the official opposition has an important role to play not only at the legislative level but also at the administrative level.
The Prime Minister himself one day stressed the value of a good parliamentary opposition. He noted the increasing complexity of the business of the state and the difficulties facing conscientious members as well as the necessity of modernizing the way in which the House of Commons deals with the business of the state.
I know the parliamentary secretary who will be rising on the subject will talk about the importance of preserving and respecting the confidential nature of corporate relationships with the various departments.
However, while trusting the executive, the fact remains that the whole thing is administered by human beings who are subject to errors; that is why it is important for our democracy that the opposition be enabled to discharge its duty. This is also the reason why the procedure is to the effect that, in some cases, members are entitled to move motions to demand the production of papers.
In a way, the government has created another department by establishing an agency called Information Canada. It is a necessary agency which will surely be helpful to the Canadian people, if it discharges its duty in an suitable manner.
Must we now create another agency for the information of members of Parliament? I hope not! That is why, on
Regional Economic Expansion behalf of the hon. member for Bellechasse, I ask for concurrence in this motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out the quite remarkable tenacity of the members of the Social Credit Party of Canada. This is the third motion of this kind moved in the House under similar circumstances.
They are of course still dissatisfied with the government's position. This is why I wish to reiterate certain points which perhaps have not been sufficiently clarified by previous interventions.
First, the government's reply is quite clear. If the documents which are demanded or at least requested are not produced it is not to deprive the opposition of an opportunity to review the merits of the grant but because of a question of privilege.
As indicated in the past, and as so competently emphasized by the member for Abitibi (M. Laprise), when an invitation is made to certain applicants, that is to say corporations or individuals interested in benefiting from the program which has been developed, it is understood that any information supplied to the department will be considered confidential.
Indeed it is indicated in the documentation gathered by the parties that the government undertakes to keep as confidential all information supplied and everyone will agree this is justified.
We must admit-and I am convinced that this is recognized by members of the Social Credit-that we still live in a country where capitalism is most important and, in fact, is the basis of our economic system. They will also admit that in our commercial exchanges, we have always accepted the necessity of maintaining discretion and keeping for ourselves the information exchanged between the parties. If the department is to discharge its duties as responsible department, it will have to obtain all available information to make its choice and take the right decision. Therefore it must be fully informed. To obtain this information the department must guarantee to the applicant that it will be kept confidential.
The same thing will happen when the member for Abitibi will see his banker and ask him to lend him some money or grant him some financial advantage. He would not like the banker to begin spreading here and there the information provided to him.
Someone argued that the member must have the information and that it must be given to him. But we use some procedures; the estimates have been mentioned, how they must be reviewed and dealt with.
Mr. Speaker, we have just completed the consideration of the government estimates.
The Social Credit Party of Canada is entitled to go to the committee on regional development to consider the estimates of that department. It rests with its members to obtain information, if there is an issue to be raised, that is any indication that in the approval of an application something was not entirely right.


Regional Economic Expansion
There are advantages. Previously, the Creditist member may have had difficulties, since the estimates were considered in the House, but thanks to the amendments to the Standing Orders of the House, the review of those estimates has been transferred to the various committees and necessarily, if anything has brought up questions to the member's mind, he might have inquired during the consideration of the estimates.
In addition, he points out that his notice of motion has been on the order paper since February 21. We have had since that date the opportunity to examine the estimates of the department. The hon. member could have then delved into the matter that interested him in view of the fact that he introduced his motion in the House through private members business.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) mentioned he was proud that the department was created and that he hoped it would expand. If he really did he sould make sure that all people who submit an application to the department are protected and that the information they will provide will be held in strict confidence. On the other hand, if the objective of the hon. member for Belle-chasse (Mr. Lambert), as presented by the hon. member for Abitibi, is to obtain or require some information I can assure him that he will obtain almost unlimited co-operation from the department.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention a case which, to my knowledge, has been a great help to my constituents: I obtained on request, with the co-operation of the department, that a seminar should be held in my riding to inform the merchants of the benefits available to them through the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and according to the reports I read, the officials did a good job and they provided all the essential information required to complete the applications. But, at that time it was clearly stated, with the public's approval, that all this information was held in the strictest confidence to the satisfaction of the people concerned.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to mention that the department has deemed it advisable, for sometime, to table in the House a monthly report which outlines the government's policy concerning the point raised by the hon. member. The table of contents of the report for April 1973 which I have at hand gives an idea of the report. Part I gives summary statistics. Part 2 deals with incentives grant activity during the month, detailing all grants. Part 3 deals with loan guarantee activity during the month and Part 4, with definitions.
Mr. Speaker, if I may, I would like to quote the third paragraph on page 2 of the Report on Regional Development Incentives of April 1973. I understand that this paragraph is reproduced in all the reports. It reads, and I quote:
The purpose of this monthly report is to provide Parliament and the general public with up-to-date information on the operation of the regional development incentives program. The report contains summary statistics on administrative actions taken from the inception of the program until the end of the month in question, together with listings of essential facts pertaining to each offer of incentive assistance accepted during that month.
Mr. Speaker, this report contains, in fact, all the information that can be given. I also note, on page 5 of the same report, another part which could be of help to hon. mem-

bers. I quote from the introduction of the report the following:
In conclusion, it should be noted that applications for incentive assistance and supporting documentation contain a large amount of information that must be regarded as commercially confidential. It is for this reason that, as a matter of policy, the department is unable to make public certain types of data. It is for the same reason that the department does not reveal the fact that a particular application has been received unless and until it results in an accepted offer of incentive assistance. This policy is, of course, consistent with the aims and objectives of the program, which is designed to encourage investment in the designated regions and special areas of Canada.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, in several cases the applicant must give the department information which could indicate a certain weakness as compared with his own competitors. Regional Economic Expansion

Therefore, the people's representative have the right and not just the privilege, to know how this money is spent, why the beneficiaries have invested it and all about this operation.
It is precisely for this positive purpose to help other industrialists and other corporations to invest more and create employment that we want to know the reasons for this investment in the Quebec newspaper Le Soleil; we do welcome it and we would like this experience to be repeated not only with newspapers but in other specific fields more in accordance with Qudbec's reality.

That does not disturb absolutely no one, and it is the money of the people from Lotbiniere, Bellechasse, Abitibi, Richmond and everywhere that is invested there, Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether, all things considered, it is not indirectly a question of patronage.

trouble, Mr. Chairman, to beat around the bush, in order to turn down a motion which is after all very simple.
If there is something to hide, then it is quite normal that they should not want to disclose such information, but if everything is above board, as I hope it is, if the investments have all been sound, Mr. Chairman, I cannot see why we should not know about them.
And I will conclude with an example: The federal government, through the Department of Economic Regional Expansion, did grant in the past a subsidy to the Manic Company, in Granby, and we know that that company went bankrupt shortly after.
Mr. Chairman, that is an unfortunate experience, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion cannot always make good investments. We understand that. However, Mr. Chairman, it is our duty as members of Parliament, to know why that has happened, to know about the circumstances, to see whether or not serious studies were undertaken before such investment was made or such grant was approved.
Mr. Chairman, to the extent that it pertains to an unfortunate experience of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, it seems to me that, as a positive approach my colleagues should agreed to this motion for production of papers, in order to know whether an investment such as the one made to the newspaper Le Soleil of Quebec could not be made also to other related, similar or different industries in our respective constituencies, as for instance to the flour mills.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, I strongly urge my colleagues and members from other parties to discharge their duty as members in a functional and effective manner, jointly and severally by asking the government to tell us exactly where the people's money goes.
When a taxpayer invests one dollar in his country by way of direct or indirect taxes, he expects, Mr. Speaker, that the government will not waste this money and that it will be invested in a profitable way. He also expects when he votes, that his representative in this House will serve as an intermediary between him and the government to check on the management of this tax dollar.
Mr. Speaker, that is precisely the role which we play and I cannot see how the hon. member from Nipissing (Mr. Blais) could blame us for fulfilling this role, while he protects the government and seems to want to hide things. As to us, we have nothing to hide, we only want to protect the people.

Mr. Speaker, on rising to speak on the merits of this motion I hesitate to follow either of the two hon. members who immediately preceded me. Each has discussed the aspects involved extensively from his point of view.
I should like, however, to make several points. On the surface, certainly, I can see the merits of a motion such as the one before us. It involves a newpaper which has an obvious influence on the public. It plays a role in judging public issues and has an influence, also, on politics. This paper finds itself receiving moneys through a program which is being run by the federal government. In these


circumstances, why, indeed, should we not produce this information if there is nothing to worry about, if there is no patronage involved.
That is a point to be considered, but I think there is an even more important principle involved here. It is the right of an individual or company not to be prejudiced by the revelation of information which might be injurious. In this instance a newspaper has received a grant and encounters criticism for doing so. Some members of the House would like to know the details respecting that grant.
It could be said in this chamber that by refusing to give these details we leave ourselves open to allegations of patronage. I say, however, that the very fact the government is not anxious to give these details is proof we have a viable reason for not doing so. Surely, if we are willing to stand up to a line of criticism which can be advanced with great strength by members of other parties and by that portion of the press which is in competition with Le Soleil, it cannot be argued that the government which I support is not being very brave in taking its present stance.
The opposition may accuse us of patronage and, perhaps, make political ground as a result. Yet we stand firm on our position. I suggest we are taking our present attitude for one main reason: If the information were made public in this one case, it would have to be done in every case. We cannot give all the details with respect to one DREE grant while refusing similar information with respect to any other organization receiving grants under this program. To proceed in such a way would result in the failure, I suggest, of the whole program-one of the most important programs initiated by the government.
The object of these grants is not to make companies wealthy. They are intended to assist them in maintaining business when their operations are in jeopardy, to help them to expand, where possible, when a reasonable request is received, but, at any rate, to continue in existence, to maintain the amount of employment they normally provide, and, hopefully, to provide additional jobs. To provide such information as the hon. member requests would prove disastrous to any grant program where the confidentiality of personal and other information is vital to the success of the organization concerned.
The officials of the department are certainly willing to discuss the case of Le Soleil with the hon. member who brought forward this motion. They maintain they are completely satisfied that there is real need in this case. If hon. members accept my general argument that a company is likely to be prejudiced in its operations by the disclosure of information of the type now demanded, does this argument not apply with even greater force to companies which find themselves in difficulty and which, because of those very circumstances, feel they must call upon an agency of government for assistance?
I understand that the dealings of the department with Le Soleil were conducted on the basis that the operation of a commercial printing undertaking was involved. Those of us who are in politics are well aware that the section of the information media concerned with printing is under serious pressure. In fact, its very existence is in question. In my own area of metropolitan Toronto we have seen a major newspaper fold. We have seen newspapers go under
Regional Economic Expansion
in New York City and other large United States urban centres. Those newspapers which are staying alive, those which I know of-and I have some experience in the media-are succeeding in doing so, except in very few extremely successful cases, by diversifying their operations. The most obvious way to diversify is to run a commercial printing operation by means of which a company can acquire stability or gain revenue independent of what may happen on the circulation side.
According to my understanding, the application made by Le Soleil was on those grounds: it was connected with their printing operation and designed to enable them to continue, something which would not be possible if they had not received this money. If a question should be raised as to the general policy followed by DREE in terms of assisting operations of this kind, may I say I have here a list of 97 different commercial printing operations across Canada which have received such assistance. This includes, for instance, Canadian Publishers of Winnipeg, Hignell Printing Limited of Winnipeg, Duha Printers of Winnipeg. The Stovell Advocate of Winnipeg also received a grant, and the name suggests to me that its operations might be compared with those of Le Soleil, the subject of the motion before us.
Let me make a further point about the difficulties faced by Le Soleil. Revealing the private business of any company seeking assistance would lead to the argument that all of us have probably faced here during private members' hour. We have all heard the argument on previous occasions on other motions, not just those moved by hon. members of the Creditiste party but motions from other parts of the House. I can recall debating one motion put forward by an hon. member for the NDP which called for the revelation of private information. All these motions which call for such information are based on the feeling of individual people that we must have answers to questions which arise in our minds.
As long as we have governments running the country there will be a question as to how much information can be revealed and how much must be retained for reasons of security or for the protection of an individual or a company. One of my colleagues suggested earlier that the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) was talking around the question and not coming to the point, or perhaps trying to talk the time out. Certainly nobody is fooling anybody else by suggesting that I am only talking on this subject because I am concerned about it. Indeed, we would be setting a very serious precedent, and destroying a very important program, if we were to let this motion go through. I make no bones about it; I am taking some time because I would find it extremely dangerous simply for us to let the motion go through.
In spite of all that has been said about a newspaper which has had some influence, we must turn the matter around and look the other way as well. The government must take certain precautions, in order to protect a principle; and that principle is the right of privacy, the right of fair business competition without your competitors knowing the details of your business, especially when you are in jeopardy and seeking assistance.


Regional Economic Expansion
There is my point in reverse. Why should a newspaper be picked upon, or why should one particular operation be placed in jeopardy, simply because the business may relate indirectly to the government? This is particularly true in this case even though this company legitimately needed assistance.
When a company seeks assistance in order to maintain itself as an operation, as is the situation in this case, the information must fall within the rules. These rules do not primarily relate to the newspaper operation but in fact to the commercial printing division.
The government will always be vulnerable to the kind of motion we are faced with today. As a backbencher I must say I always have some sympathy toward this kind of motion moved by members of parliament who are not in the government party but are honestly seeking information. I understand their situation when they believe something may be suspect. This is especially true when they are seeking information seemingly, as argued by one hon. member earlier, not on the basis of something crucially important, and not because they smell something very rotten in the woodpile, but simply because they want to know the facts and understand the situation.
I suggest it is not that simple. If we let this one insignificant motion go through during this private members' hour, during the middle of a hot summer, we will be opening up a can of worms, particularly in respect of those companies who might want to come to the government seeking assistance, trusting that the information they provided would be private. We would be starting a domino effect which would destroy the ability of the government to deal with the private affairs of any individual or company in order to assist them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier in the session the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEac-hen) brought down a series of guidelines which were designed to provide the government with methods by which motions for the production of papers would be judged. One of the main criteria was the question of confidentiality of internal documentation and the confidentiality of information exchanged between governments and the private sector. This includes not only companies but also the sanctity of income tax forms and other information which one gives the government, for example at census time.
What we are dealing with almost every time we debate private members' motions for the production of papers is this question of confidentiality and the question of trust. We really have not come to any solution which is satisfactory to us all. We have not come to any solution to which we can point with some pride that takes into account, on the one hand, the needs of the government and the private sector to exchange information on a confidential basis, and on the other hand, the needs of legislators to have access to the kind of information which is brought forth to governments at this time. One of the frustrations we have as legislators is that we do not have access to all the information that is truly available on any given subject. Sometimes that information is confidential and does exist, but sometimes that information simply does not exist at all.

We have referred these guidelines of which I spoke earlier to the Standing Committee on Statutory Instruments. That committee is going to make an examination as to how these guidelines have operated in the six months they have been accepted by the House. We have been making an investigation into the way in which questions on the order paper and motions for the production of papers have been treated by various government departments in order to ascertain if in fact there has been a significant change in the amount of material being made available by the government which was not the case before, or whether government departments are carrying on in their merry old way of keeping information secret largely for the sake of keeping it confidential and away from others.
This is a very important point because it is the intention of the authors of the guidelines to open up, so far as practical, information which the government collects, sometimes by accident and sometimes deliberately, and make this information available not only to legislators but also to the general public.
The way to do this is not yet known. The amount of information which any government department has at any given time is simply mountainous. The question of determining how much of that information should be made available without request and how much should be made available on request, how much should be made available for limited circulation and what part of it ought to be kept secret in the interest of confidentiality and of the state, is a question on which, I suspect, there will be no conclusive judgment simply because it amounts to a judgment by individual men.
The standards in this regard change. The standards of today will not necessarily be the standards of tomorrow. Today we probably release more information by way of these motions, and just on general principle, than was the case 10 years ago. Mr. Speaker, I see it is six o'clock.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Drury that Bill C-196, respecting the 1976 Olympic games, be read the third time and do pass, and the amendment thereto (Mr. Peters, p. 5978).

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin my remarks tonight on this bill regarding the 1976 summer Olympic games by saying


this bill runs counter to the solemn promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a few months ago regarding these games. I refer to the statement made by the Prime Minister in this House to the effect that the city of Montreal must bear the full burden of the financing of the games and that under no circumstances would the people of Canada be asked or required to foot the bill for any deficit incurred by either the city of Montreal, the Olympic committee or the province of Quebec.
Members of this House will recall that Mayor Drapeau of Montreal stated at the time he was successful in getting the games for Montreal that it was his victory and that it would be his responsibility. He not only stated he would not ask the federal government to pay off the deficit on the operation of the games, but repeatedly assured us that there would be no deficit. However, we find in this bill clear evidence that there has been some sort of consultation between the federal government and Mayor Drapeau, and possibly the government of Quebec, concerning the games.
We also find clear evidence in this bill that the federal government has in fact committed the people of Canada in direct contradiction to the Prime Minister's solemn promise. We find that the federal government has committed itself in several ways in respect of the financing of the games, and now in this House of Commons we are asked to formalize these commitments. This has been done without the formality and without the courtesy of a statement by the government that the Prime Minister's promise was not really a promise at all. The people of Canada have been committed to financing the games without being told in advance that all the solemn assurances to the contrary were in fact a put-off.
I cannot help but think consultations were taking place along these lines at the same time as we were told the federal government had adopted a hands-off policy in respect of the financing of the games. Before I go into the specifics of the schemes that have been worked out to try to raise money to finance the games, I should like to refer my colleagues to clause 11 (1) which states:
There shall be established in the accounts of Canada an account to be known as the Olympic Account.
Further along, subclause (3) states:
There shall be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund and charged to the Olympic Account
(a)	all administrative, merchandising, distribution, promotion and other costs incurred by Canada in connection with the distribution and sale of Olympic coins, as determined by the Postmaster General; and
(b)	all amounts paid to the Olympic Corporation pursuant to subsection (4).
We find that subclause (6) allows the federal government to authorize payments out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund to the extent of $500,000. This is a far cry from the position the Prime Minister adopted a few months ago and announced in this House. We in this House, and the Canadian people, were reassured by that announcement on the position and policy of the government. But I cannot help feeling that members of this House are going to be asked some very searching questions by their constituents when the full impact of this bill is felt across the country.
Olympic Bill
I can well remember the hoopla and the fanfare that attended Mayor Drapeau's pyrrhic victory in having the summer games awarded to the city of Montreal. He was hailed as the super salesman from that city, and many people even compared him to the great P. T. Barnum. At that time I was apprehensive, even though Mayor Drapeau assured one and all that he would take care of everything. For one thing I was not so naive that I could accept the thesis that Mayor Drapeau could commit the city of Montreal to host an international event of this magnitude without in some way committing the federal government of Canada.
On February 9 of this year I told my constituents in a news letter that Mayor Drapeau had in fact committed the Canadian people and the Canadian government when he committed Montreal to host the games. I have been proven right, Mr. Speaker, but the mere fact of being right on this point does not make me feel any less apprehensive. In my view, this has been a shabby and devious way for the federal government and the Mayor of Montreal to work out the details of financing the games.
I stated at the time the games were awarded to Montreal that I was under the impression that Mr. Drapeau had assured the Olympic committee that he had worked out the financial details as far as the games were concerned; that the committee had been shown some facts and figures, together with a comprehensive plan setting out procedures to cover housing, games facilities, security and all other pertinent aspects of holding the games.
We now know that that was not the case. In retrospect we can be forgiven for believing that Mayor Drapeau had in fact committed the federal government on such matters as financing, security, housing and other matters. We saw recently, for example, that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation got into the picture very quickly, and that there will be tens of millions of dollars available in CMHC money to finance the construction of housing for the athletes at the games. This is a major item of expense, and it clearly shows that the federal government has been deeply involved in the Olympic games for quite a long time, long before this bill was drafted, and certainly a long time before the bill was introduced in the House.
Here I want to say just a word about security at the games. In this aspect I will have to agree with my colleague to my left, the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose), who stated it was common knowledge that the matter of security is beyond the capability of the police forces of Montreal and the province.
This means that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Canadian Armed Forces will have to be involved. The recent experiences of other countries holding the Olympic games show clearly that security is one of the most important aspects of the games. In fact, Mr. Speaker, surveys have shown that a great many Canadians are against holding the games in Canada because of the unhappy experiences of countries such as Mexico and Germany.
There are radical groups in the world today who plan ahead to the Olympic games. They use them as platforms to vent their hatred on countries that they feel have


Olympic Bill
slighted them, or have prevented them from expressing honest and legitimate views. Whether these people are right or wrong as far as their beliefs are concerned is immaterial; the fact is that they are prepared to commit murder to disrupt the games and publicize their grievances.
I will not dwell on these matters any further, Mr. Speaker, because as we all know by now these aspects of the games have been worked out by the city of Montreal and the federal government. I will only say, before I deal with the amendments that have been added to the bill by the standing committee, that I wish the government had taken us into its confidence back in the early days of the negotiations.
However, Mr. Speaker, I am relieved to be able to say to my constituents that an amendment to the original bill limits the extent to which the Olympic Corporation can dip into the public till-"trough" is a better word. This has been set at $260 million, but I am not certain in my own mind that this is going to be enough to finance such an ambitious undertaking. I am reminded of the experience we had with Expo 67, and I am rather uneasy, to say the least.
Going back to clause 11, I note that the net cost of the redemption of any Olympic coins left unsold will be charged to the Olympic account. This is not exactly a guarantee. It will only serve to identify another item in any deficit that occurs in the financing of the games, and this will be picked up by the federal government. It will have to be paid off by the federal government because there simply is not anyone else to whom Mayor Drapeau can turn.
The taxpayers should take some comfort from the amendments that make up the whole of clause 13. These amendments call for periodical reports from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) concerning the progress of the selling, redemption and production of Olympic coins. This is a refreshing departure from the way in which the Expo 67 accounting was handled, and it will also allow for regular accounting of the amounts of money paid into the account of the Olympic Corporation.
I am also relieved that reports filed by the government concerning the Olympic coins account can be referred to a standing committee for scrutiny if a motion to do so is signed by at least 60 members and is filed with the Speaker of the House. I have no doubt that from time to time there will be 60 members who are interested enough to take the trouble to petition for a committee examination of these reports.
We would not be debating such an important matter as hosting the Olympic games in this atmosphere of distrust and animosity if the government had come clean with us several months ago. It should be apparent to everyone directly concerned with the games that it would have been far better for general public acceptance of the games if the federal government and the city of Montreal had not been carrying on these negotiations as though it were a private and personal deal.
This is a public matter, Mr. Speaker, and I must say to the House and to all of the principals in the proceedings that, as long as Mayor Drapeau persisted in grandstand-

ing, the federal government should have kept its hands out of the stew. We were assured by the Prime Minister during that period that that is exactly what it was doing. However, we now know that during this grandstand play the mayor was being backed, supported and abetted by the federal government.
That is the reason we are going to have to buckle down now and try to convince the Canadian people that the Olympic games will be conducted in the very best traditions of Canadian hospitality, Canadian ingenuity and Canadian sportsmanship. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill proposes an ingenious method of achieving the objective of self-financing the 1976 summer Olympics without cost to the taxpayers. If it succeeds, it may inspire a new slogan, "Play now-pay never," because it will mean that a mammoth spectacle can be produced without an equally mammoth subsidy from the government.
It sounds almost too good to be true, and members of the public as well as of this House may be pardoned if they doubt it can be done. Even the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has had his moments of uncertainty. On August 15, 1972, in a letter to Mayor Jean Drapeau, the Prime Minister said that in spite of repeated requests by federal officials the government had not received any detailed information about how the games were to be financed. On February 24, 1972, the mayor had estimated the cost would be about $124 million, but in August the Prime Minister said a federal government cost analysis estimated the cost might be about one half billion dollars, four times the mayor's estimate.
On January 23, 1973, uncertainty about financing the games was still perplexing the Prime Minister. In a letter to the mayor, he pointed out that the city of Montreal and COJO had approved capital and operating budgets of $310 million. That meant an increase in five months from an estimate of $124 million to $310 million, an escalation of two and one half times. The Prime Minister informed the mayor that federal officials feared operating expenditures would be greater than those projected in the COJO budget and that revenue sources for financing capital works would yield $100 million less than was previously expected. The result would be a deficit of between $100 and $200 million, assuming that costs would not escalate between 1973 and 1976.
On the basis of this gloomy prospect, the Prime Minister indicated the government could not accede to any request for federal authorization for revenue producing schemes, such as issuing coins and stamps and holding lotteries. That might have stopped a lesser man than the mayor of Montreal. Many might well have expected this meant the end of the Olympics.
Just eight days later, however, the premier of Quebec wrote the Prime Minister to say that the federal government would not have to assume the interim financing of costs relative to the games during the period leading up to and including the holding of the games. Provided the federal government agreed to remit to COJO the net proceeds of the sale of these special coins and stamps, premier Robert Bourassa agreed the federal government would not be asked for any special contribution toward the cost of the games.
My reason for citing this correspondence is to emphasize how commitments have been made that must inhibit either Montreal or Quebec from coming to the federal government for any further assistance. Mr. Roger Rousseau, the Olympics commissioner, has outlined his hope that the games will be self-financing if parliament passes Bill C-196. I hope he is right, but he may not be, so it must


Olympic Bill
be made absolutely clear to the premier, the mayor and the Olympics commissioner that if their costs exceed their revenue, they cannot look to this government and this Parliament for more help.
We are mindful of the way the costs of Expo '67 escalated. Parliament had to pay a subsidy far in excess of what had been anticipated. That kind of escalation must not happen again, and there should be no doubt left in the minds of officials in Montreal or Quebec about the determination of Ottawa to hold the line.
This is not because taxpayers in the rest of Canada are unwilling to share in the cost of this great spectacle. They are already committed to sizeable federal expenditures. Costs of building the Olympic village will involve CMHC funds estimated to range from $26 to $54 million, and that project will be of permanent use to the city of Montreal.
A Treasury Board financial analysis on January 31, 1973 estimated that the cost of Armed Forces involvement in the program of the games would be $8 million; that the cost of the R.C.M.P. and other federal employees attached to the games would be $20 million, and that the cost of CBC services would be around $25 million. The total is a possible $107 million of federal money, according to 1973 costs. That should indicate the way in which people across this country are supporting the project, even though it is only a few years since they paid the deficit for Expo amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars.
Will the people be asked for still more? The Premier of Quebec has told the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) that they will not. This assurance, however, has been given in the face of a Treasury Board forecast that revenues from all sources, including the games, will be $172 million less than costs: a possible deficit of $172 million. Where will this money come from? No one has answered that question except to claim the sale of the coins, the stamps and the lottery tickets, added to regular Olympic revenues, will be so great that there will be no deficit.
What a promise! What a vision! If the scheme works, I suggest all party leaders offer to serve in a coalition government under Jean Drapeau. He will be the first man in Canadian history ever to have achieved so much for so little, and he is obviously the man this country needs. If we can finance games this way, why not housing, why not roads, why not parks? Why limit such brilliance to so short a display?
Let us just suppose the scheme does not work. Has the Premier of Quebec made any commitment that his government will assume the deficit? Has the mayor of Montreal indicated how much his city could underwrite? Just as important, has the Prime Minister of Canada made any arrangements for federal authorities to supervise and audit the way COJO's funds are managed? If the government is investing $107 million in the games, surely it is entitled to some voice in their management. In spite of all these assurances, by 1976 or 1977 a new mayor of Montreal and a new premier of Quebec may approach a new prime minister of Canada to lift them out of a hole they will claim others dug for them.
[Mr. Stackhouse.)
Surely the federal government should be playing a much more active role in the management of this massive event. I suggest the government appoint an auditor general to keep a close eye on how the money is spent by COJO, and who could do it better than Mr. Maxwell Henderson himself?

The amendments to Bill C-196, accepted in committee, have made it a better bill because they have provided for more government supervision of the coin issue. They have provided safeguards which could prevent the coins being misused in such a way that COJO could pay off its debts with Olympic coins. They have set a limit on the aggregate amount so as to prevent the coin issue from being so great it could debase the currency.
I think this is the right approach. One option which I believe the NDP favours would be to defeat the bill, a move which could seriously jeopardize the possibility of the games being held. Another option, and a better one, is to accept this measure, but to demand much more efficient management or administration so that the promised result of the schemes put before us would be more likely to be achieved.
We need to be mindful of the value of the games to the entire nation. They give us an opportunity to return the hospitality our athletes have received in Olympics held in other countries when other countries have assumed the cost and the burden of those events. They afford us an opportunity to unite this country in one great experience, as a result of which athletic development will be stimulated in every community. Several speakers criticizing the Olympics have pointed out that various local communities need arenas, stadia, swimming pools and the like. I believe these communities have much more hope of achieving those ambitions because of the inspiration and stimulus they will receive from the games.
It is therefore incumbent upon us to do what is required of us at this time; that is to say, not to jeopardize the possibility of these games being held but to take action which would lead to their realization; not to sink the Olympics, but to take the steps needed to assure the efficient administration of the project's finances.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to speak during this debate on the motion for third reading of Bill C-196.
I have followed attentively the various steps this bill went through, first in this House and then in the parliamentary committee. I must admit, Mr. Speaker, that I personally feel greatly satisfied when I think that Parliament is about to authorize the Post Office and also the Royal Canadian Mint to proceed with the issuing of Olympic stamps and coins this year as well as during the next three years, so as to provide for the financing of the 1976 Summer Olympic Games.
Through such issues and the lotteries that will be established, the Canadian government is going into a unique undertaking which-I emphasize it-is unprecedented in the history of Olympic Games financing.


I should like tonight to raise six points that were brought forward by members and which deserve explanations.
First I should like to say very clearly that the government wants this bill to be approved.
Second, I should like to remind all hon. members that the government members have taken every possible means to accelerate the passage of this bill.
Thirdly, I would like it to be clearly understood that the government's attitude about this bill has never changed and its enthusiasm has never wavered.
Fourthly, to those who are wondering what support the government will give the Games, I would like to remind them, by listing a host of cases where the government has shown how efficient it can be, that in fact it will play an extremely important role in the success of the Olympic Games.
Fifthly, I would like to say that in spite of the wish expressed by some hon. members, the Canadian government cannot substitute itself to the city of Montreal in the organisation of the Olympic Games proper.
Finally, I would like to invite all hon. members to realize that the 1976 Olympic Games are a unique opportunity to promote Canadian unity and rekindle the enthusiasm that prevailed in 1967.
Mr. Speaker, let me say that it is quite clear that the government wants this bill to be passed within the shortest possible time. My colleagues from the cabinet, the Liberal members of Parliament, all save one maybe, as well as many members of our party, from all the provinces, have repeatedly expressed their support of the Games.
Now I would like to point out to the House that differences of opinions are allowed within our party. The statements made by my colleague from Matane (Mr. De Bane) were those of a private individual and not those of a government representative. He spoke as any member of our party can speak in this House or outside. His opinion is a personal one quite exceptional within our group. The ministers, the members, the rank and file throughout the country have repeatedly given their unconditional support to the Olympic Games and I think that the position of the Government and of the Party I am representing is quite clear in this connection.
Furthermore, I would like to say that we did our best in an attempt to speed up the passage of this legislation. During the debate on second reading, government members restricted their remarks. In committee, there were very few contributions from the government side and this, in order to allow opposition members to express their views and ask all the questions they wanted.
I even recall a sitting when several government members gave up their allotted time to the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) who had the floor practically all the time.
Finally, government members co-operated fully, first, in the drafting and, secondly, in the passage of some of the amendments moved.
Olympic Bill
It is beyond doubt that, as far as we from the government side are concerned, we have been ready to support and pass this bill for a long time.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize this: the government's position and enthusiasm with regard to the Olympic Games have remained the same since May 1969, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) officially endorsed the application made by the City of Montreal to the International Olympic Committee. Therefore, this government's position has been known from the start. The federal government, while supporting the application of Montreal, said it could not share in the costs of the necessary facilities and related infrastructure. I think that the Prime Minister's letter to the Mayor of Montreal is quite clear in this respect, and I quote:
Dear Sir:
I am pleased to send you a copy of a letter that I sent to the President of the International Olympic Committee in support of the City of Montreal which is seeking the honour of hosting the 1976 Summer Olympic Games.
However, the federal government having already provided, within the framework of EXPO, substantial contributions for various facilities, some of which can also be used for the Olympic Games, I am sure that you understand that we cannot give financial support to the organization of the Games or its promotion.
Now, this position has not changed. Ottawa has been supporting Montreal for the holding of the Games since the beginning. The federal government states that it will keep its promises, that it will do its duty, but that is all. And I disagree with the comments made earlier during the debate by the member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) who said, and I quote:
-it is Canada which has chosen Montreal as the city which will represent our country for the 1976 Olympic Games . . . therefore we must not make any mistake . . . In view of the secretive manner in which the Prime Minister has handled all this from the beginning.
Mr. Speaker, I want to make it clear that there has been no secret dealings or underhand practices behind this. The formal statements of the Prime Minister are very clear, and at no time have we tried to go through the back door in order to do some things or to prevent some things from being done. The position is quite clear and I think that it is very well understood by both Montreal and the Olympic Committee.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot help stressing-and with malice to none-that the attitude of the Progressive Conservative party towards the Olympic Games has been, to say the least, confused and even quite involved, especially in the last election. At that time, the official opposition party took great care not to take an official stand on the 1976 Olympic Games. Instead, the hon. members opposite were suggesting a national policy on sports as vague as could be. I admit, however, that their position has become clear during the debate on this bill and I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) on the remarks he made in this House. I wish he could have a good influence on all his colleagues so that they will all use the same frank and strong language, because, unfortunately, we have heard far too many inconsistencies in the remarks of some of his colleagues on this bill.
Mr. Speaker, we have been taken to task and maybe we still are, because in some cases, we are unable to give at


Olympic Bill
this stage specific guarantees about the anticipated revenues through the sale of Olympic coins and stamps. In the same breath, our colleagues opposite blame the government for allowing the Royal Canadian Mint to get ready for the minting of these Olympic commemorative coins.
On the one hand, Mr. Speaker, the opposition members who sat on the committee spoke abundantly about the shameless deficit that will be incurred by holding the games. On the other hand, they presented an amendment for the sole purpose of limiting the amount of money that will be handed to the Olympics Committee.
After speaking at length and very highly about the games, they presented an amendment which would greatly limit the possible financing of those games by setting at $450 millions the total value of coins that could be minted and circulated.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, some members of the opposition sharply accused the government of not wanting to finance the games directly. However none of them wished to move an amendment which would have modified Bill C-196 that way.
Nevertheless, I welcome the support of a very large majority of members from the official opposition.
I am glad they took such a position and I wish to tell them that I fully expect their most thorough co-operation when the time comes to promote the sale of coins and stamps limited and issued with this Parliament's authorization.
I would also like to say, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian government will play an extremely important and foremost role in the success or the failure of the 1976 Olympics. This government is ready to do what should be done to ensure that this undertaking meets with the most complete success. The international scope and the fall-outs that will result for Canada imply a concern on the part of the government at the level of services connected with the games, which are of federal jurisdiction. That is how the participation of federal departments will take place normally and to a great extent without involving any extraordinary expenses.
I can say that about fifteen departments will be directly or indirectly concerned with the organization of the Olympic Games of 1976.
First of all, the Department of External Affairs will be responsible for the formal arrangements occasioned by the visits from numerous foreign dignitaries, and will provide valuable assistance for the coordination and advertising of the Games through our embassies. As a matter of fact, His Excellency General Commissioner Rousseau has been loaned by this Department to the Organization Committee of the Olympic Games.
The Manpower and Immigration Department through its Manpower Centres will help COJO when recruiting casual employees required for the Games. The Immigration Division will also be involved in the coordination of the entry into this country of the numerous athletes, officials and visitors.
As far as the National Defence Department is concerned, it will provide the necessary security in connection with the numerous sporting events.

The Department of National Revenue will share in the reception of visitors by providing the necessary additional staff.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police, under the jurisdiction of the Solicitor General, will carry out the very important duties of security co-ordinating body in co-operatin with both provincial and city police forces, in Montreal as well as in Kingston.
Other government agencies will fulfill their normal responsibilities and take an active part in the holding of the games. Suffice it to say that the Departments of Environment, Agriculture, Industry, Trade and Commerce, Public Works as well as Information Canada and various other agencies will lend a precious and helping hand in the organization and holding of the games.
I should like to say a few words on the matter of federal services and agencies which will result in major expenses which, by the way, have already been made public and which will be incurred within the next three years.
In the vital field of security, the federal government is responsible for providing the Olympic Games with security arrangements capable of ensuring the protection of
9,000	athletes, some 4,000 journalists and more than 250,000 spectators who will see the games every day.
The government has also allocated a grant of some $25 million to the CBC which, at the broadcasting agency of the host country, will look after the radio and television coverage of the Olympic Games.
This money will enable all Canadians to watch the various competitions at home thanks to radio and television. To the very many foreign commentators who will cover the games for their own countries we will offer a complete range of radio and television facilities. It is estimated that over one billion people across the world will receive reports on the Olympics Games from Montreal in 1976 and by the same token get to know better our wonderful country.
Finally, the funds allocated under CMHC programs will depend on the number of housing units built in the Olympic village and will be paid out to the extent that those units will meet the usual standards of the corporation.
I would also like to stress the importance of the role that will be played by the department of National Health and Welfare which, without making any direct financial contribution to the organization of the Olympic Games, will also participate in a very important way through Sports Canada in their preparation. Assistance programs for the preparation of teams, the training of referees and judges, the organization of clinics, and travel and shelter grants for Canadian athletes participating in national and international competitions are as many accomplishments already underway. That department will also be subsidizing national amateur sports associations which will organize competitions across the country in coming years.
The "Mission 76" co-ordination committee will ensure that our Canadian athletes can participate in international events in order to acquire preparatory experience for the 1976 games. Thus our young Canadians will go to the World Student Games in Moscow next August, the Com-


monwealth Games in New Zealand next February and the Pan-American Games in Chili in 1975. They will also have the opportunity of participating in competitions to be held domestically, particularly the Canada Summer Games which will be held in coming days in New Westminster and Burnaby, British Columbia.
Mr. Speaker, I want to say that the government of Canada responded to the request made by the city of Montreal and the Olympic committee by drafting the bill before us. This act will make it possible to collect revenues through the issue and sale of special commemorative stamps and Olympic coins as well as through the organization of a national lottery. In this way, the government will ensure the basic financing of the Olympic Games without taxing directly the Canadian taxpayer.
As all hon. members know, the Post Office Department will issue commemorative stamps to mark the staging of the 1976 Olympic Games. The first series of stamps, if the government passes this bill in the next few days, will be issued on September 20. These will be the first two stamps of a series of very high quality stamps which we intend to issue. These two stamps will have low nominal value, i.e. the value most frequently used to pay postage.
As minister responsible for the sale of the Olympic commemorative stamps and coins, I should like to reassure hon. members and all Canadians who could be somewhat apprehensive as to our issuing programs and the means that will be used to provide for their sale in Canada as well as abroad. First I should like to tell them that a marketing advisory committee will be set up and include all the people concerned in this coin program, including the federal departments and COJO.
I should like to tell them also that I will have the pleasure of leading a group of experts who will supervise all aspects of marketing within a new branch that my department will create for those special programs.
With the help of those two groups of sales experts and thanks to a market study and a publicity promotion, I am confident that the Canadian government will be very aptly and sensibly advised as to its sales program, its marketing methods and as to the choice of the institutions and agents who will co-operate in the sale.
May I be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to reiterate my confidence in those prospective sales. We rely very much upon the international market and our program has already aroused much interest in foreign countries. Half of our production will probably be sold in North America and we have every reason to believe that we can rely on a great number of clients in the wealthiest countries in Europe and Asia.
There is throughout the world an increasing interest in precious metals and their products, such as coins. The intrinsic value of our collectors' items and of our numismatic samples will be such that Canadian Olympic coins will surely draw the attention of the whole world.
The collectors' market is very large. We shall direct our efforts towards that sector of the market that is already obviously interested in such articles, be they of a numismatic or philatelic nature. Moreover, we can count on the interest of all Canadians who will see in these issues an
Olympic Bill
opportunity of directly supporting the Olympic Games and to do so freely here, in this country.
It must be realized once and for all that these Olympic coins and stamps will give all Canadians a unique opportunity of supporting the games and pave the way for other countries that cannot now hope to finance the games but that will some day be able to through the self-financing procedures that Canada will have been the first country to attempt successfully.
In conclusion, I would like to say to many members who would like the Canadian government to serve as a substitute for the City of Montreal and assume the entire responsibility for these games that it is in fact a city which is getting the games, assuming the responsibility for them, taking the task of building the required facilities. A country cannot therefore act as substitute for a city, according to the criteria of the international organization committee of the Olympic Games and there we must follow the long established rules of the International Olympic Committee.
I feel the time has come for this House to support what the COJO and the City of Montreal have been asking us for a long time, namely to support a bill allowing selffinancing of the 1976 Olympic Games.
I am convinced that the 1976 Games will offer all Canadians, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, a splendid opportunity to make a national effort without equal since the extraordinary festivities of our 1967 centennial. All Canada and especially our youth, can prove one more, at the Olympic Games, that our national pride and will to excell are without equal, in the world.
We had this great feeling when we watched the performance of an athlete like Karen Magnussen or those of Team Canada during the Russia-Canada series. We all had this warm feeling of satisfaction in seeing these Canadians take up the challenge of the best athletes in front of the world.
I am convinced that all Canadians from coast to coast will relive these same emotions, these same sensations during the Olympics Games of 1976.
I therefore invite all hon. members to join in this Canadian endeavour in which the whole world will see another proof of Canadian initiative and unity.
The hour has come for all Canadians to co-operate. I therefore ask all hon. members to rally round us as soon as Bill C-196 has won the support of the majority.
