speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight not to delay unduly the debate on the Olympic bill but to congratulate the Mayor of Montreal for bringing the games to Canada. In this he has shown great ingenuity. We should all be proud of athletic progress in Canada wherever it takes place. In many quarters the method of financing approved by the federal government is deemed to be devious. But if the system works, members of all parties will be happy.
I rise tonight to say that we in Edmonton, Alberta, are going to host the 1978 Commonwealth games, and I would like some assurance from the government that we in the


Olympic Bill
city of Edmonton will be treated with kindness equal to that which we on this side have shown to the holding of the Olympic games in Montreal.
It is not too early to start planning for the Commonwealth games. Over the past year a number of people in Edmonton have worked hard to get those games for Edmonton. The Exhibition Association is now in the process of building a coliseum, and again I hope the minister will give me some assurance that the people of Edmonton will be given consideration equal to that shown the people of Montreal.
We in Edmonton are proud that we have some outstanding athletes. Those athletes will develop if we hold the Olympic games and Commonwealth games in Canada. I repeat, I hope the minister will give an assurance tonight that the same consideration will be given to the Commonwealth games in Edmonton in 1978 as is given to the Olympic games in Montreal in 1976. I would not have risen tonight had I managed to ask the minister for this assurance during question period this afternoon, but I rise now and ask him if will he give that assurance.

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am certainly not the only member of parliament to have received a number of letters over the past year and a half objecting to the holding of the Olympic games in Canada because, it is argued this country cannot afford the cost, which is estimated at somewhere between $300 million and $500 million.
I am opposed to the holding of the Olympic games not because Canada cannot afford that kind of expenditures, and not because I am opposed to the encouragement of sports and recreation. I am opposed to the Olympic games because I believe, on the basis of our past experience, that we will do quite poorly in the 1976 Olympics. We will do poorly simply because we have not had the facilities in this country to provide proper training for our young people, our potential athletes. We do not have fully qualified coaches to develop the skills of our athletes.
If we want to compete in international sport and at the same time avoid our athletes having a poor record and somewhat disgracing the country, then I believe we must build the necessary facilities to allow our young people the training they must have.
I am not opposed to the expenditure of $300 million to $500 million on athletics, but I am opposed to the expenditure of that kind of money in one city. I would oppose it whether we had the Olympics in Vancouver, Toronto, Hamilton, Winnipeg or Montreal. I think Canada should spend something in the neighbourhood of $200 million to $300 million on building sports facilities in all the major cities of the country. Let us have Olympic size swimming pools and diving platforms in Vancouver, Edmonton, Calgary, Regina, Winnipeg, Hamilton, Halifax. Let us also have track facilities in those cities. Let us have hockey rinks. Let us not forget that the best hockey players in this country barely beat the Russians in that relatively recent competition.
That is what we need, not expenditures in one city. I would like to see us do for sports what was done for the 
arts some years ago through the Canada Council, and that is set up a trust fund of $100 million or $200 million. That way we would not have to depend on a particular government or a particular minister to provide the money required for a real program to train the coaches needed in the various athletic competitions that are held during the Olympics. Let us have a fund and use what it earns each year to train the coaches.
It has been suggested that we ought to approve this bill because Montreal needs an economic boost, that it has been left behind in the competition with Toronto and Toronto is growing faster. Neither I nor members of this party have ever oposed any proposal to improve the economic or social life of Montreal or any other city. If the vote were to allocate $300 million or $500 million to improve living and working conditions in the city of Montreal, we would support it. Montreal has tens of thousands of children living in houses which are a disgrace to any modern city. Yet what we are proposing is not to give CMHC the financial resources to encourage Montreal to build public housing units, but to give Montreal, through CMHC, enough money to build an Olympic village which will house something like 10,000 or 15,000 athletes and related personnel. We do not know how many of these units will be allocated for public housing, but on the basis of the experience of the United States we do know that if it were to be devoted to public housing it would end up as a ghetto to breed crime and everything else.
Montreal is a city of 2'/2 million people which dumps almost 100 per cent of its sewage into the St. Lawrence River-untreated sewage. If the proposal were to spend federal money to help Montreal build a modern sewage system, not a single member of the New Democratic Party in Parliament would oppose it. What we are opposing today and will vote against is the expenditure of a substantial amount of money in one city, the city of Montreal, in a way which we believe to be completely wrong.
We are not against sports, we are not against Montreal, we are not against Quebec, but we believe that to hold the Olympics anywhere in Canada in 1976 is a mistake. We believe that the money that the people of Canada will be required to pay in one way or another could be better spent in this country, and better spent in the province of Quebec. Because we believe that, Mr. Speaker, we intend to vote against this bill.

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I bow to my colleagues; I know they will be interested in what I have to say. If there was an Olympic medal to be given for kicking the can, I am sure it would be won by a member of this House. As a matter of fact, I think the best way to end this debate would probably be to give out a few medals. I should like to recommend that the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Langlois) be considered for a medal for "jumping to conclusions". During our committee meetings he displayed great skill and style, and it is a matter of record that he jumped to more conclusions than anyone else on the committee.
Probably the most outstanding performer of all those on the committee was the hon. member from Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose). He not only beat all his party colleagues, but he had the fastest about-face in the time trials. Not only did he about-face, he turned himself inside out while


doing an about-face. Even the most experienced gymnasts blanch at the thought of such a feat.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, you will agree that an about-face in itself is extremely difficult, especially for a member of the NDP. We find the hon. member for Fraser Valley West on February 2, as reported at page 899 of Hansard, saying:
My party welcomes the statement by the Prime Ministei (Mr. Trudeau) today in which he took some trouble to outline the parameters of federal involvement in Canada's first Olympic games. We wish our first Olympic games every possible success as a potentially great moment in the history of our nation.
He went on to talk about keeping to budget and said he looked forward to Canada leading the way to staging the Olympic games on a budget scale. But when this bill was brought into this House on second reading, the hon. member for Fraser Valley West, whose only sporting credentials are that he owns a jock strap and has athlete's foot, led a spirited battle against staging the Olympic games in Canada.
Then to show off to all who cared to see, after pleading in February for Canada to lead the way in staging a "budget Olympics"-that is his term, Mr. Speaker-after pleading for economy, we find him voting against an amendment to limit the amount paid to the Olympic committee through the sale of coins. How can you compete against talent like that? So I award him a medal, Mr. Speaker. I think he deserves it. As for his colleague, the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Harney), well, he led the way in committee with points of order and deserves at least an honourable mention for his efforts.
Of course, we could not have really made much progress with this bill had the stage not been set by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He started the bill on its way with considerable confusion, which is normal. Many hon. members recall our early questions about the Olympics in January of this year, just after this Twenty-ninth Parliament opened. Hon. members will recall the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) directing a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), only to be told he did not answer for the Olympics. They will then recall several questions being put to the right hon. the Prime Minister about the Olympics. The answers were obscure and contained little information, which again is normal. Then in reply to direct questioning he told a surprised House that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) would answer questions on the Olympics.
Well, now, this was clearly no way to start off on the Olympics. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs wears slip-on shoes because he cannot tie his shoelaces. That is about par for the course.
After watching the performance of the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) when he appeared before the committee, we really should award him a medal for being the most evasive witness. His footwork was fantastic. He would say one thing, then another, then contradict the first statement; then, when pressed, he blamed it all on the translation. Anyone who attended the late sittings will recall how the hon. members opposite barked when the Postmaster General commanded. When he shook his head they placed their gags in their mouths.
Olympic Bill
Of course, we all know about the famous letters from the Prime Minister to Premier Bourassa, Mayor Drapeau and Mr. Rousseau, and the famous guarantee replies he waved before the House before he tabled them. As the hon. member for York Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) pointed out, they have little legal value and would not stand up in court.
If we could give a prize for a sloppy bill, we would award it to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury). He should also be given honourable mention for his efforts on the silver blades. He skated all around the bill, and it appeared to many of us that he was wrongly placed for he was clearly more evasive than was the Postmaster General. But he did his compulsory figures well, except they did not add up. He could not explain the difference in the budget drawn up by the Olympic committee and his own Treasury Board. After two nights of skating around the problem, someone whispered in his ear that the Olympic committee would run a lottery and settle the deficit in this way. I think that official deserves honourable mention because the minister at that point was about to throw in the towel.
The events we watched were amazing. We learned that coins which are to be minted are to be sold at a discount. Never in our history have we sold our money at a discount, so we put in an amendment to stop that.

speechtext: What happened?

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
We learned that COJO was classed as an amateur athletic association and would be eligible for grants under the Fitness and Amateur Sport Act. There is a slick way to balance the budget. We will have to watch it, and will have to watch future estimates submitted by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The hon. member for Fraser Valley West drew our attention to this in committee; I commend him for that.
Then, to our surprise, we found that Bill C-196 was open-ended. There was no limit as to the amount of coinage that could be minted, so we put an amendment in to cover that. We also found that there was no limit on the profit or seigniorage that could accrue to COJO, in spite of the fact that COJO had asked for a specific amount of money. So we covered that with an amendment.
As well, we defined by way of an amendment what was meant by postal related products, as this term was unclear even to the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet). All in all we submitted six amendments and one new clause. The bill only had 12 clauses; it was printed on six pages. We made several significant changes to the bill. We put in several safeguards and generally made the bill a little more palatable than it was when we had first read it.
The committee meetings were the worst I have attended. The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) remarked that they were the worst meetings he had attended in 20 years. The turning point came about two o'clock one morning, after a particularly bitter meeting. The hon. member for Laval (Mr. Roy) had previously blown the meeting by confusing the hand signals of the Postmaster General. The President of the Treasury Board and the Postmaster General stood talking to two members of my party at two o'clock in the morning. I will not betray the confidences of


Olympic Bill
private conversations, but the two ministers at this point realized we really wanted the bill passed, and that some straight talk was necessary with no more "fancy Dan stuff". We just wanted straight talk from here on, or it would be no show.
From that point we made good progress, and the bill was in due course amended. It passed through the committee stage and came before this House on the report stage. The tragedy of the bitterness that was evident at the committee meetings was really all unnecessary. If the President of the Treasury Board or the Postmaster General had had any foresight, they would have circulated an information paper and avoided much of the time spent in debate in committee. They would have had an explanation at hand to explain the difference between the COJO budget and the Treasury Board budget. The Postmaster General would not have had to hide behind the translators. The Master of the Mint could have told us openly that he had proceeded in February to design the Olympic coins; he could have revealed his authority for such action and thus saved the committee much time.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say that all this is behind us and I think it would be better if we ended this debate on a conciliatory note. When this bill passes we will see the people at COJO swing into action. I wish them well. I hope that the Olympics in 1976 are a great success. I hope we will be able to capture some of the spirit of the games. I hope that those who expressed doubts about the financial aspects of the Olympics will be proven wrong. We want the Olympics to succeed. We hope the Olympics will become a symbol to the young people of this country and to the world.
We hope that all those persons of the press who have up to now been overly critical of the Olympics will, with the passage of this bill, climb on board and help us to make the 1976 Olympics a success.

-in the name of all competitors I promise that we will take part in these Olympic Games, respecting and abiding by the rules which govern them in the true spirit of sportsmanship, for the glory of sport and the name of our teams.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
Someone says I have five minutes. I will try to be brief. I do not think the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) needs defending. Someone said he is inconsistent. I remind the House that consistency is the hobgoblin of tiny minds. It seems to me the hon. member was flexible enough to examine this bill carefully and see

the tremendous holes which have developed in it since we first looked at the financing of these games.
Many here have said that they are not opposed to the Olympic games but are opposed to the method of financing. I do not speak for my party when I say that I am opposed to the Olympic games, regardless of the Mickey Mouse method of financing that has been brought forward. Even a cursory review of the history of the last two games ought to convince anyone that they make no real contribution to international understanding.
When you remember, Mr. Speaker, the assassination of the Israelis at the Munich games and the slaughter of Mexican students in the 1968 games, you realize that the games do nothing whatsoever to advance or encourage the health of participating athletes. If the games do not do either of these things, why should we bother with them? It will be far better to restructure the Olympics and eliminate the national chauvinism that goes with the games than tolerate them as they now are.
Let us look at the effect the Olympics will have on this country and compare them with the kinds of national athletic events that we ourselves sponsor outside the international field, events like the one in my riding. I am referring to the Canada summer games in New Westminster. For a federal investment of less than $2 million, 3,000 athletes will participate. How many Canadian athletes will participate in the Olympic games?

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext: Many.

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
What real contribution will we make to national fitness through these games and with this fantastic investment of money?
The hon. member for Saint Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) said this afternoon that the games are desirable because there is too much emphasis on professionalism in this country I agree. The Olympics do not represent amateurism; they represent "shamateurism," and we have known it for a long time. The Olympic oath is more honoured in the breach than otherwise. The Olympics are simply another extension of professional sport; and it is appropriate that the edifices which will be created for the games and funded by the people of Canada will probably be used for professional football and professional baseball in Montreal.
The hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) said that we should not worry so much about the lack of community facilities since the facilities to be built will stay after the games. I think it is far better to spend the money this way and advance the cause of genuine community sport than spend it on the kind of wasteful extravaganza that is to take place.
If we spent that same amount of money on Montreal and the surrounding area in providing facilities, we could have Olympic champions for the next 40 years instead of the wasteful circus that is going to take place.
The comment has been made that this is an anti-French position. On the contrary, this is a pro-French position. It is the kind of position that supports the provision of money for thousands of people in Quebec who are denied adequate community facilities. Instead of giving them these, we are giving them circuses. I was delighted with


the speech of the hon. member for Matane (Mr. De Bane). His attitude towards these games is genuinely patriotic. He understands the true social significance of what is being done with regard to those games.
I want to read part of an editorial that appeared in the Windsor Star. I quote:
Canada should seriously consider the implementation of this sports-for-all program. The demand for sport facilities is there, the goals are desirable, and most important, the concept of financing the program with would-be Olympic funds should be agreeable to the taxpayer.
I believe it is time for the government to abandon the Olympic Games, subdue its hysterical concern to develop Olympic athletes, and place emphasis on public recreation.
Sport is not for the elite performer-it is for everyone.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-SUGGESTED PROVISION OF SHUTTLE SERVICE BETWEEN TORONTO-MONTREAL AND TORONTO-OTTAWA
AIR TRANSPORT-SUGGESTED PROVISION OF SHUTTLE SERVICE BETWEEN TORONTO-MONTREAL AND TORONTO-OTTAWA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to discuss the implications of the question I addressed recently to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-chand) on the subject of the shuttle service between Toronto and Ottawa. More than 1400 passengers fly back and forth by Air Canada between those two cities on any typical business day. Their number will increase as each year the nation's capital becomes the place where businessmen must come for negotiations with, and decisions from, a growing number of federal agencies which are making this city the head office of almost every enterprise in Canada. It is therefore time we looked more closely at ways of improving the vital air link between these two cities, each of them a political and financial capital.
One improvement might be a shuttle service, since it is often difficult for a person to know when his business in Toronto or Ottawa will be finished. He may make reservations only to find he must stay longer. Then he must attempt new reservations, which often are difficult to arrange, and on some days, such as Friday, impossible. The advantage of the shuttle would be that the individual would know that at certain times planes would be leaving and that he would have a number of chances to get a flight to Toronto or Ottawa.
Shuttle services are provided now by Eastern Airlines in a network that links Boston, Washington, Newark, New York and Montreal. In the Montreal-New York shuttle, each passenger is guaranteed a seat on the plane. When a plane fills up, another is provided so that no one is left standing at the terminal. In spite of this guarantee the cost is no greater than that of the economy flight on Air Canada from Montreal to New York. Thus, anyone travelling between those cities knows that at scheduled hours he can get a flight just by showing up at the terminal with his $34.
Pacific Western Airlines runs a shuttle between Calgary and Edmonton. It does not guarantee a seat to everyone who shows up but at peak times it does add extra planes. At rush hour times it provides a flight every half hour. Both privately-owned companies inform me that their shuttle services are operating in the black, Pacific Western having operated the Calgary-Edmonton shuttle for many years.
I therefore urge the minister to recommend that Air Canada look again at this proposal. If there is good reason why it should not be tried out in the Toronto-Ottawa service, I recommend this compromise: let Air Canada add extra planes during certain rush periods, or, at least, let it provide a shuttle in Toronto's terminal No. 2, itself almost a mile long. The present jitney service is totally inadequate. Often the cars are not working; never are there enough. Surely the ministry of transport can do as good a
Adjournment Debate
job at terminal No. 2 as the House of Commons buses do for M.Ps here. If the minister cannot give us a shuttle between Ottawa and Toronto, let him at least give us one between one end of terminal No. 2 and the other.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ian Watson (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-SUGGESTED PROVISION OF SHUTTLE SERVICE BETWEEN TORONTO-MONTREAL AND TORONTO-OTTAWA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, further to the hon. member's question about domestic shuttle service possibilities between Toronto and Montreal or Toronto and Ottawa, I should like, first of all, to elaborate on the rapid air system which is now in effect between Toronto and Montreal.
A year ago Air Canada introduced the rapid air system in order to better serve the local needs of Toronto-Mont-real passengers. Although the rapid air system is not a full shuttle in the open, no reservations sense, those people who do show up without reservations are usually accommodated on the flight of their choice. Most of the exceptions occur at peak traffic time, when passengers with no reservations may have to wait for one or more flights. Rapid air is, however, a very frequent service, contrary to U.S. shuttle services which tend to operate every hour or two. Rapid air offers an average of 22 flights per day in each direction.
A shuttle is just one of the number of ways of carrying passengers, but it cannot be introduced without taking into account the travel demands of the public at large. For example, many of the flights now operating as part of the rapid air system carry passengers beyond Toronto and Montreal to other parts of the country. Scheduling these passengers through the Toronto-Montreal corridors has been beneficial to them because it has permitted greater flight frequency to these other points. Similarly, the local Toronto-Montreal passengers have benefited because these through flights have meant a more frequent rapid air schedule.
In addition to rapid air, in the past year Air Canada has introduced an innovated pricing structure on domestic services that has lowered average fare levels considerably, mainly through general fare reduction on long-haul services and through all peak 30 per cent "Explore Canada" fare discounts on long and short-haul services.
These two programs demonstrate that Air Canada does its best to provide the best possible service at the lowest possible prices, and I am advised that further improvements can be expected over the next year.

subtopic: EXHIBITIONS-EXPO '74, SPOKANE, WASHINGTON- REASON FOR FAILURE OF CANADA TO HAVE PAVILION
EXHIBITIONS-EXPO '74, SPOKANE, WASHINGTON- REASON FOR FAILURE OF CANADA TO HAVE PAVILION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon in the House of Commons I asked the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Sharp) why Canada had decided not to participate in Expo '74 which is to be held in Spokane, in the State of Washington, in view of the fact that months ago Canada indicated that a Canadian pavilion would be constructed for Canadian exhibits. I also asked the minister if the government would reconsider its position on this very important matter.
6028


Adjournment Debate
In replying to the question the minister indicated that the government had given the matter a great deal of careful study and had come to the conclusion that there were other and more important priorities for the $1.5 million than the building of a Canadian pavilion at Expo '74.
In my frank opinion the government has received some very poor advice in regard to this matter. I do not know what kind of study was carried out, but it looks to me as though some civil servants tucked away in a ministerial office in Ottawa have again scratched out an important project simply because they knew very little about it. This is another example of federal bureaucracy ignoring important issues in Canada.
It is my intention this evening to outline for the minister a number of reasons why I feel the government should re-consider its position on this very important matter.
The first point I would like to make is that a Canadian pavilion at Expo '74 would be an excellent investment as far as favourable publicity for Canada is concerned. There will be many hundreds of thousands of visitors to Expo '74 from all over the United States and many other countries. The excellent opportunity which this offers to publicize our country and its many assets should not be passed over. Spokane is very close to the Canadian border and a number of Canadian exhibits to advertise what our country has to offer in the way of tourist attractions could generate tens of millions of dollars in tourist revenue, even during the time the exposition was in progress. It seems to me that this one major aspect alone is well worth the investment involved.
The tourist industry has become a major revenue-producing asset for Canada. We spend vast sums of money at every level to promote it. Canadian scenery is something we can sell over and over again without depleting the resource, yet when a major opportunity presents itself to us to really promote our scenic grandeur, at a time when many hundreds of thousands of visitors will be within a short drive of the Canadian border, we find our federal government unaware of the opportunities presented by Expo '74.
A Canadian pavilion would not cater only to tourism. It could be the display centre for our arts, crafts and a host of other Canadian skills which we wish the world to know about. This investment in a pavilion would be the most economic and effective type of advertising that any country could devise. It is not a one-shot affair, for the advertising carries over for several months. This is something the federal government should not take lightly.
One of the most disappointing aspects of the federal government's short-sighted decision will be the feeling by many western Canadians that once again Ottawa has failed to help promote western Canada, which stands to gain most by Expo '74 and any federal participation in it. It is discouraging to the large number of organizations in British Columbia and Alberta which have been promoting Expo '74 to realize that our federal government wants to have no part of it. If private organizations and provincial departments realize the value of Expo '74 to the Canadian scene, then surely the federal government can make funds available for a Canadian pavilion and give some real leadership in promoting it.

There are many other aspects which enter into the picture of Canadian participation in Expo '74, including that of good public relations with our neighbour to the south. It seems rather odd that the Canadian government, after committing itself to participate in Expo '74, suddenly decides that a Canadian pavilion cannot be built. No doubt some reason can be advanced for the federal decision, but it will appear to many Canadians to be just another weak federal excuse to overlook Canadian interests, especially in the west.
There is another aspect of Expo '74 which I would like to bring to the attention of the government. A Canadian pavilion would mean a large number of jobs for young Canadians over a period of several months. A major increase of tourists to Canada during this period would also result in a large number of additional summer jobs for young Canadians. Active promotions by means of federal participation in Expo '74 could be a major factor in improving the job situation, and this aspect should not be overlooked.
Time does not permit me to expand further on this topic, Mr. Speaker. Frankly I feel the federal government has made a serious mistake by withdrawing from its proposed participation in Expo '74. I would urge the minister and the government to immediately reconsider the decision made yesterday and I trust that any reconsideration will result in a Canadian pavilion at Expo '74.

subtopic: EXHIBITIONS-EXPO '74, SPOKANE, WASHINGTON- REASON FOR FAILURE OF CANADA TO HAVE PAVILION

Mr. Speaker, I feel it would be most difficult not to agree with the hon. member when he speaks of the benefits of Expo '74. The problem lies in the cost, and I feel that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) gave the hon. member quite a clear answer this afternoon.
As he explained, Canada's participation in the Spokane World Exhibition on the human environnment was studied in detail, and we reached the conclusion that in view of the budgetary restrictions of the government, earmarking credits in the order of $1,850,000 to that end would not be justifiable in 1974. This having been said, I am sure we all hope that Expo '74 will be a real success.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAY-QUEBEC-OBLIGATION OF EMPLOYEES IN PASSENGER SERVICE TO BE BILINGUAL
CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAY-QUEBEC-OBLIGATION OF EMPLOYEES IN PASSENGER SERVICE TO BE BILINGUAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I put to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) on July 19, 1973, which is reported in Hansard at page 5782, reads as follows:
Can he tell the House if the employees of the Canadian National in the Quebec passenger service must be bilingual?
Since I did not get a reply, I want to point out to the House, and in particular to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), that it is unthinkable that in 1973, one should have to ask such questions, after the Canadian government spent millions of dollars to promote bilingualism.
Mr. Speaker, there is at this time in Quebec an explosive political climate in respect of language problems. There-


fore, what is the federal government doing about this ticklish matter? Let me give you some examples of the way Quebecers are treated.
Some of my constituents have complained that CNR employees in the passenger service could only speak English. Others have complained that some governmental services in the National Capital had no bilingual staff.
Also what about departments which are looking for English-speaking unilingual employees saying nothing of messengers who suffer from blatant injustice? By that I mean that there is no difference in pay for a bilingual messenger as compared with an English unilingual one. The same situation prevails for the security personnel of the House of Commons.
I received another complaint this morning; the Public Works Department is advertising an open competition, bearing No. 73-PW-CR-CC-15, for hiring a foreman for various jobs. It is provided on page 3, in the language requirements section, that knowledge of English is essential. Nothing is said about requirements concerning the French language. It seems that this is the procedure followed by most departments with respect to the working language; it is a strange way to implement the language policy announced in this House some time ago.
The purpose of my intervention, Mr. Speaker, is not to play politics, but rather to point out to the government the frequent inadequacies which are observed in all departments so that the leaders of this country may be fair and equitable to all Canadians, whatever their culture.
The government's behaviour which I denounce now is but provocation aimed at French speaking Canadians. Let us recall that during the 1968 general elections, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) would enjoy talking to Quebecers about his so-called policy of bilingualism and his just society.
Ever since that time, his promises have fallen into oblivion, as though in a deaf ear. The same applies, by the way, to all the election promises made over the past hundred years.
I shall take a few more minutes to denounce also some opposition members who, during the last election campaign, used French Canadians as a springboard to win seats in some Western ridings at the expense of other parties.
Mr. Speaker, I dare not use the words that are coming to my mind in these circumstances; but I wish all hon. members to know that if I speak tonight it is in an effort to make this government realize the necessity of protecting the unity of our country.
Before my election to this House as member for Rimous-ki, I was often inclined to condemn certain French-Canadians who were saying that life in French Canada
Adjournment Debate
was dreadful. Today, I understand and I can tell where separatism originated from. Wherever they are, to my left, to my right or in front of me, in this House, I have been able to spot the real agitators since the beginning of this session.
In future years, we will have to try by all the means at our disposal to find solutions to enable all Canadians of whatever culture to live in a healthy atmosphere favouring understanding between the different groups so that our people may be against segregation.
In conclusion, I ask the House, Mr. Speaker, to keep a careful watch over our national unity, if we want the Quebecers to keep on paying taxes to allow the federal government to continue its grants to Western Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ian Watson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAY-QUEBEC-OBLIGATION OF EMPLOYEES IN PASSENGER SERVICE TO BE BILINGUAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am speaking tonight on behalf of the Parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Guay) who is not in Ottawa today.
Since the fall of 1968, all new employees hired to work on passenger trains in the province of Quebec must be bilingual pursuant to agreements concluded with the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway, Transport and General Workers as well as with the Brotherhood of Railway Workers.
Currently, the situation in the province of Quebec may be summarized as follows: out of a total of 416 employees in the passenger service and meal service, only 50 are unilingual English-speaking people, i.e. only 25 out of 150 employees working in passenger trains; however, the latter have at least followed a French course of 17 days.
I am informed that the seniority agreements with the unions involved prevent-for these employees hired prior to 1968-the Canadian National from forbidding the few English-speaking unilingual employees to fill in the passenger trains certain positions which they are entitled to occupy because of their seniority.
However, we are assured that the passenger train services are always provided in both official languages.
It is to be noted that the previous information concerns the St-Lawrence region.
Other trains in Quebec are staffed by personnel from Toronto or Halifax. In both those cities, the knowledge of French is being improved progressively for the personnel likely to work on trains travelling through Quebec, through an appropriate hiring policy and especially French courses.
A bilingual service is offered by the Canadian National at all its passenger stations.
I wish to thank the hon. member who just rose-
